stem: The external wall of a house of timber frame construction has the following specification: External render thickness 19 mm; Concrete block outer leaf thickness 100 mm; Oriented Strand Board (OSB) sheeting thickness 18 mm; Timber stud inner leaf thickness 120 mm; Mineral wool insulation between studs thickness 120 mm; Plasterboard thickness 12.5 mm. Thermal data of outer leaf and cavity: Resistance of the external surface (R) 0.048 m2 °C/W; Resistivity of the external plaster (r) 2.170 m °C/W; Conductivity of concrete block (k) 1.320 W/m °C; Resistance of the cavity (R) 0.170 m2 °C/W. Thermal data of inner leaf: Conductivity of OSB sheeting (k) 0.130 W/m °C; Conductivity of mineral wool (k) 0.040 W/m °C; Conductivity of plasterboard (k) 0.160 W/m °C; Resistance of the internal surface (R) 0.104 m2 °C/W. Note: The timber studs of the inner leaf need not be considered in your calculations.
questionText: Calculate the cost of heat lost annually through this wall, using the following data: Area of external wall 150 m2; Average internal temperature 18 °C; Average external temperature 6 °C; U-value of wall as calculated above; Heating period 8 hours per day, every day for 38 weeks per annum; Cost of oil 96 cent per litre; Calorific value of oil 37350 kJ per litre; 1000 Watts 1 kJ per second.

rows.contextNote: Heat loss = U-value × area × temperature difference = 0.273555 × 150 × 12 = 492.39994 watts (joules per second).
Heating period = 60 × 60 × 8 × 7 × 38 = 7,660,800 seconds (2,128 hours).

rows.verbatim: Litres of oil for one year

rows.contextNote: Annual cost = 100.99 × €0.96 = €96.96. The scheme’s alternative one-line method gives €96.94.

questionText: It is proposed to upgrade the thermal properties of the above wall to meet the Passive House standard by fixing expanded polystyrene to the external surface. Given the thermal conductivity (k) of expanded polystyrene as 0.037 W/m °C, calculate the thickness of expanded polystyrene required to achieve a U-value of 0.15 W/m2 °C.

rows.contextNote: Required resistance = 1 ÷ 0.15 = 6.6666 m²K/W.
Existing resistance = 1 ÷ 0.27356 = 3.6555 m²K/W.
T = 3.0111 × 0.037 = 0.1114107 m: 111.4 mm of expanded polystyrene (111 or 112 mm accepted).

questionText: Minimising heat loss and storing heat gain are important considerations in Passive House design. Using notes and freehand sketches, show best practice design detailing to minimise heat loss and maximise heat storage in a Passive House for any two of the following: foundations; ground floor; walls.

rows.contextNote: Any two of the three printed items, each notes 6 and sketches 6 = 12. Foundations: a passive foundation of U-value 0.10–0.15 W/m²K with no thermal bridges; high compressive strength insulation; a traditional strip with autoclaved aerated concrete blockwork. Ground Floor: thermal mass from a thicker screed and tile finish to absorb and retain heat; high insulation; no thermal bridges; airtightness. Walls: a passive wall of U-value 0.10–0.15 W/m²K; high insulation, no thermal bridges, airtightness; a block inner leaf with plaster for thermal mass, or heat stores such as a Trombe wall in timber frame.

questionText: Explain, with the aid of notes and freehand sketches, any five of the following: lever valve; mortice and tenon joint; cob wall; thermal bridge; dual flush toilet; smart meter; solar gain; low-e glazing; access ramp.

rows.contextNote: Explain any five of the nine terms. Each term is marked separately: primary communication of relevant information 6 and other communication 4, in notes or sketches (the scheme reserves no fixed split between them). Lever valve: controls the flow of water with a single lever operating a hollow ball; the lever shows the valve open when parallel to the pipe and closed when perpendicular; a good seal; various diameters. Mortice and tenon joint: used in doors, windows and furniture: a mortice cut in one piece and a tenon, about a third of the thickness, formed on the end of the other to fit it. Cob wall: clay, straw or hemp mixed with water (sometimes lime or sand), built in layers on a coursed stone base, each layer dried before the next; tapered and finished with lime render. Thermal bridge: a bridge in the insulation, at floors, cills, lintels, jambs or roofs, conducting heat out; higher heat loss, condensation and mould; prevented by continuous insulation. Dual flush toilet: a cistern with two buttons: about 6–9 litres for solid and 3–4 litres for liquid waste, cutting water use and the water sent to treatment. Smart meter: records and shows the electricity used in the home and its cost, giving the householder control; may be topped up; can also record water or gas. Solar gain: free heat from solar radiation entering through glazing, stored in masonry as a heat sink; maximised by orientation, insulation and airtightness; the main principle of passive design. Low-e glazing: a thin transparent metal or metal-oxide coating on the panes that reflects heat back into the house while admitting solar gain; dearer but reduces heat loss. Access ramp: a sloping path for easy access for wheelchairs, buggies and people with restricted mobility: gradient about 1:20, at least 1500 mm clear width, sections no longer than 9.0 m, non-slip and well lit.

questionText: Explain, with the aid of notes and freehand sketches, any five of the following: handrail; box dovetail joint; purlin; damp-proof course; ball valve; energy rating; wind turbine; joist hanger; service cavity.

rows.contextNote: Explain any five of the nine terms. Each term is marked separately: primary communication of relevant information 6 and other communication 4, in notes or sketches (the scheme reserves no fixed split between them). Hand rail: the solid member fitted to the newel posts, parallel to the pitch line, carried on the balusters; generally 75 × 50 mm, jointed to the newel by mortise and tenon, 900–1000 mm above the pitch line. Box dovetail joint: a joint of tails and pins for box shapes and drawers in high-quality furniture, by hand or with jigs; dovetail slope 1:6 in softwood and 1:8 in hardwood; decorative with contrasting woods. Purlin: the member under the rafters giving them support and alignment in a traditional cut roof, typically 175 × 75 mm, carried on struts to an internal load-bearing wall or on a steel joist. Damp-proof course: an impermeable barrier, usually heavy plastic, in external and internal walls, linked to the damp-proof membrane, 150 mm above ground; stops rising damp and damp crossing the cavity at openings. Ball valve: controls the water entering a cistern or tank: a float rises with the water and closes the valve; mounted on the side of the cistern and connected to the supply. Energy rating: labels rating appliances, and homes through the Building Energy Rating, from A (most efficient, lowest bills) to G, to help consumers choose. Wind turbine: converts wind energy to mechanical energy and then electricity through its blades, generator and tower; small or large scale, sited for the wind; an eco-friendly source of energy. Joist hanger: a galvanised steel hanger wrapping three sides of a joist end, nailed or screwed through predrilled holes, anchoring floor, ceiling and decking joists; stronger than nails alone. Service cavity: a separate cavity on the inside of an external wall carrying wiring and plumbing so they do not damage the airtightness membrane; used in solid and timber frame walls.

stem: A house built in the 1970s has an uninsulated solid concrete ground floor, as shown, with a sand/cement fine screed finish.
questionText:
Calculate the U-value of the uninsulated concrete ground floor, given the following data: Sand/cement fine screed thickness 50 mm; Concrete floor slab thickness 100 mm; Radon barrier thickness 0.25 mm; Sand blinding thickness 40 mm; Hardcore thickness 200 mm; Subsoil thickness 300 mm.
Thermal data of the concrete ground floor: Resistance of internal top surface of floor (R) 0.104 m2 °C/W; Resistivity of fine screed (r) 0.710 m °C/W; Conductivity of concrete floor slab (k) 1.280 W/m °C; Conductivity of radon barrier (k) 0.250 W/m °C; Conductivity of sand blinding (k) 0.160 W/m °C; Conductivity of hardcore (k) 1.350 W/m °C; Conductivity of subsoil (k) 1.600 W/m °C.

rows.contextNote: The calculation set out in a table of material, conductivity, resistivity, thickness and resistance.

rows.verbatim: Internal top surface resistance Fine screed Concrete floor slab Radon barrier Sand blinding Hardcore Subsoil
rows.contextNote: Seven resistances, 3 each, by R = T/k (or R = T × r for the screed): internal top surface 0.1040 (given); screed 0.05 × 0.71 = 0.0355; slab 0.1/1.28 = 0.0781; radon barrier 0.00025/0.25 = 0.0010; sand blinding 0.04/0.16 = 0.2500; hardcore 0.2/1.35 = 0.1481; subsoil 0.3/1.6 = 0.1875. All in m²°C/W.
Total resistance Rt = 0.8042 m²°C/W.

rows.verbatim: Calculation of U-value of ground floor
rows.contextNote: U = 1 ÷ Rt = 1 ÷ 0.8042 = 1.2434 W/m²°C, with units.

sourceMaterial.presentationNote: All printed data are retained in the original question. Parts (b) and (c) use the U-value from (a); the scheme’s worked answers are U = 1.2434 W/m²°C, an annual cost of €352.50 and 216.9 mm of expanded polystyrene.

questionText: Using notes and freehand sketches, discuss the importance of any two of the following in Passive House design: space heating energy demand; building form; thermal bridging.

rows.verbatim: Design of a passive house - any 2
rows.contextNote: Any two of the three printed items, each notes 4 and sketches 4 = 8. Space heating energy demand: the energy to keep 20 °C all year, at most 15 kWh/m²/a in a Passive House, set by insulation and airtightness; solar gain from well-placed glazing with shading against overheating. Building form: a simple compact form with fewer junctions, less envelope and lower heat loss; a low surface-to-volume (A/V) ratio, ideally 0.7 or less; avoid complex hips and valleys. Thermal bridging: areas of higher conductivity let heat escape and cause cold spots, condensation and mould; continuity of insulation at openings, floor and eaves junctions, as in the scheme’s details.

stem: The external wall of a house built in the 1990s is of 100 mm concrete block construction with a 100 mm partially filled cavity, as shown.
questionText:
Calculate the U-value of the wall, given the construction has the following sequence and data: External render thickness 16 mm; Concrete block outer leaf thickness 100 mm; Clear cavity width 50 mm; Polystyrene insulation thickness 50 mm; Concrete block inner leaf thickness 100 mm; Internal plaster thickness 12 mm.
Thermal data of the external wall: Resistance of external surface (R) 0.048 m2 °C/W; Resistivity of external render (r) 2.170 m °C/W; Conductivity of concrete external blockwork (k) 1.440 W/m °C; Resistance of clear cavity (R) 0.170 m2 °C/W; Conductivity of insulation (k) 0.037 W/m °C; Conductivity of concrete internal blockwork (k) 1.440 W/m °C; Resistivity of internal plaster (r) 6.250 m °C/W; Resistance of internal surface (R) 0.122 m2 °C/W.

rows.contextNote: Eight resistances, 3 each, by R = T/k (or R = T × r for render and plaster): external surface 0.048 (given); render 0.016 × 2.170 = 0.035; external blockwork 0.1/1.44 = 0.069; clear cavity 0.170 (given); insulation 0.05/0.037 = 1.351; internal blockwork 0.1/1.44 = 0.069; plaster 0.012 × 6.25 = 0.075; internal surface 0.122 (given). All in m²°C/W.
Total resistance Rt = 1.939 m²°C/W.
U = 1 ÷ Rt = 1 ÷ 1.939 = 0.516 W/m²°C, with units.

Given the thermal conductivity (k) of expanded polystyrene as 0.031 W/m°C, calculate the thickness of expanded polystyrene required to achieve a U-value of 0.15 W/m2 °C.

rows.verbatim: Resistance for U- value for 0.15Wm2K (using R=1/U)
rows.contextNote: Required resistance = 1 ÷ 0.15 = 6.666 m²K/W.

rows.verbatim: Resistance from calculated U-value from part (a)
rows.contextNote: Existing resistance = 1 ÷ 0.516 = 1.939 m²K/W (the scheme prints the divisor as 0.156).
Difference = 6.666 − 1.939 = 4.727 m²K/W.
T = 4.727 × 0.031 = 0.146537 m: 147 mm of expanded polystyrene (146 or 147 mm accepted).

sourceMaterial.label: ORIGINAL QUESTION 5
sourceMaterial.title: Cavity wall U-value, heat-loss cost and external insulation
sourceMaterial.attribution: SEC Leaving Certificate Construction Studies 2019 Higher Level — © State Examinations Commission.
sourceMaterial.presentationNote: All printed data are retained in the original question. Part (b) uses the U-value from (a); the scheme’s worked answers are U = 0.516 W/m²°C, an annual cost of €199.60 and 147 mm of expanded polystyrene.

stem: A house built to nZEB standards has a highly insulated solid concrete ground floor with a hardwood finish, as shown.
questionText:
Calculate the U-value of the floor, given the construction has the following sequence and data: Hardwood flooring thickness 20 mm; sand/cement fine screed thickness 65 mm; floor insulation thickness 200mm; concrete floor slab thickness 150 mm; radon barrier thickness 0.25 mm; sand blinding thickness 40 mm; hardcore thickness 200 mm; subsoil thickness 300 mm.
Thermal data of the ground floor: resistance of internal top surface of floor (R) 0.104 m2 ⁰C/W; conductivity of hardwood flooring (k) 6.666 W/m ⁰C; resistivity of fine screed (r) 1.410 m ⁰C/W; conductivity of floor insulation (k) 0.022 W/m ⁰C; conductivity of concrete floor slab (k) 1.280 W/m ⁰C; conductivity of radon barrier (k) 0.250 W/m ⁰C; conductivity of sand blinding (k) 0.160 W/m ⁰C; conductivity of hardcore (k) 1.350 W/m ⁰C; conductivity of subsoil (k) 1.600 W/m ⁰C.

rows.contextNote: Nine resistances, 3 each, by R = T/k (or R = T × r for the screed): internal surface 0.104 (given); hardwood 0.02/6.666 = 0.003; screed 0.065 × 1.410 = 0.092; insulation 0.2/0.022 = 9.091; slab 0.15/1.28 = 0.117; radon barrier 0.00025/0.25 = 0.001; sand blinding 0.04/0.16 = 0.25; hardcore 0.2/1.35 = 0.148; subsoil 0.3/1.6 = 0.188. All in m²°C/W.
Total resistance Rt = 9.993 m²°C/W.
U = 1 ÷ Rt = 1 ÷ 9.993 = 0.10 W/m²°C, with units.

sourceMaterial.label: ORIGINAL QUESTION 5
sourceMaterial.title: Ground floor U-value, heat-loss cost and thermal bridge
sourceMaterial.attribution: SEC Leaving Certificate Construction Studies 2020 Higher Level — © State Examinations Commission.
sourceMaterial.presentationNote: All printed data are retained in the original question. Part (b) uses the U-value from (a); the scheme’s worked answers are U = 0.10 W/m²°C and an annual cost of €18.62.

stem: A house built to nZEB standards has a highly insulated solid concrete ground floor with a hardwood finish, as shown.
questionText: Using the U-value of the floor obtained at 5(a) above and the following data, calculate the cost of heat lost annually through this floor: dimensions of floor slab 6.5 metres × 9.0 metres; average internal temperature 20 ⁰C; average temperature of subsoil 6 ⁰C; heating period 9 hours daily for 39 weeks per annum; cost of oil 96 cent per litre; calorific value of oil 37350 kJ per litre; 1000 Watts: 1 kJ per second.

rows.contextNote: Heat loss = U-value × area × temperature difference = 0.10 × 58.5 × (20 − 6) = 81.9 watts (joules per second).
Heating period = 60 × 60 × 9 × 7 × 39 = 8,845,200 seconds (2,457 hours).

rows.verbatim: Litres of oil for one year

rows.contextNote: Annual cost = 19.39 × €0.96 = €18.62. The scheme’s alternative one-line method gives the same €18.62.

questionText: Explain, with the aid of notes and freehand sketches, any five of the following: stud partition; domino joint; slump test; dynamic glass; pyrite; pile foundation; trimmer; butt hinge; solar panel.

rows.contextNote: Explain any five of the nine terms. Each term is marked separately: primary communication of relevant information 6 and other communication 4, in notes or sketches (the scheme reserves no fixed split between them). Stud partition: a timber or metal stud frame fixed to the floor, ceiling and walls; vertical studs at 400 mm centres between head and sole plates, braced by noggins and covered with plasterboard; load bearing or non-load bearing. Domino joint: a woodworking joint cut with a domino joiner, used in modern furniture to butt, edge or corner join pieces of wood quickly; very strong with wood adhesive. Slump test: measures the workability of fresh concrete on site, batch by batch, and checks the water content; a truncated cone, tamping rod and meter stick; 0–50 mm slump low workability, 50–75 mm medium. Dynamic glass: a thin coating that changes from clear to tinted under a small DC voltage (electrochromic) or with the sun’s heat (thermochromic), reducing glare and overheating for the occupants’ comfort. Pyrite: a naturally occurring iron sulphide in sedimentary rock that cracks and expands when exposed to moisture and oxygen; in fill under a building it heaves ground floors and cracks walls. Pile foundation: supports and anchors a building where the soil has low bearing capacity or good soil is deep; end-bearing, friction or short-bored, drilled and poured or driven; a ground beam carries the walls onto the piles. Trimmer: a joist supporting the ends of trimmed joists or rafters around a stairwell or chimney opening, carried by trimming joists; carries more load, so usually 25 mm thicker than common joists. Butt hinge: a widely used hinge of two leaves and a central pin, 12–150 mm long, in brass, mild steel or stainless steel; the leaves sit in shallow trenches and are fixed with countersunk screws; for doors, windows and boxes. Solar Panel: evacuated tubes converting solar radiation to heat, or photovoltaic panels generating electricity; best on a south-facing roof at about 45° in Ireland; a sustainable source that cuts CO2 emissions.

stem: The sketch shows a proposed external wall design detail for a new house of timber frame construction.
questionText: It is proposed to redesign the above timber frame wall and upgrade its thermal properties to meet the Passive House standard by adding sheep wool insulation to the design of the internal leaf. Given the thermal conductivity (k) of sheep wool insulation as 0.034 W/m ⁰C, calculate the thickness of additional insulation required to achieve a U-value of 0.15 W/m2 ⁰C.

rows.verbatim: Resistance for U- value for 0.15 W/m2 °c (using R=1/U)
rows.contextNote: Required resistance = 1 ÷ 0.15 = 6.666 m²°C/W.

rows.verbatim: Resistance from calculated U-value from part (a)
rows.contextNote: Resistance of the wall from (a) = 1 ÷ 0.184 = 5.424 m²°C/W.
Difference = 6.666 − 5.424 = 1.243 m²°C/W.

rows.verbatim: Required thickness of insulation in mm.
rows.contextNote: Additional sheep wool = 42 mm (42 or 43 mm accepted). Alternative calculation methods are acceptable.

questionText: Explain, with the aid of notes and freehand sketches, any five of the following: joist bridging; steel reinforcement; biscuit joint; working drawing; heat pump; room thermostat; rooflight; ridgeboard; building energy rating.

rows.contextNote: Explain any five of the nine terms. Each term is marked separately: primary communication of relevant information 6 and other communication 4, in notes or sketches (the scheme reserves no fixed split between them). Joist bridging: keeps floor joists vertical and stops them twisting; stiffens and ties the joists together and spreads load to neighbouring joists; solid or herringbone bridging. Steel reinforcement: combined with concrete as reinforced concrete, taking the tension in load-bearing members; placed low in a foundation; patterned bars (rebar) or mesh for grip, tied into cages. Biscuit joint: used in modern furniture for butt and edge joints in boards of different widths and thicknesses; pressed beech biscuits fit grooves cut by a biscuit joiner, giving a larger gluing area. Working drawing: a scaled drawing used as a guide when building furniture or buildings, with elevations, plan and sections, dimensions and notes; hand drafted or CAD; often called plans or blueprints. Heat pump: moves heat from one place to another, such as from the outside air or ground into the house for heating and hot water, very efficiently. Room thermostat: senses the room temperature and switches the heating to keep it at the chosen level; dial, digital or smart (Wi-Fi) control; lower heating bills and less waste. Roof light: a window in the roof surface for natural light, double, triple or quadruple glazed; lets an attic become a usable room; more privacy than a dormer. Ridge board: the horizontal member at the top ends of the rafters forming the apex of a cut roof; rafters are nailed to it; supported by the rafters or gables; typically 225 × 32 or 225 × 25 mm. Building Energy Rating: a certificate rating a home’s energy performance from A to G, calculated on the energy for space heating, hot water, ventilation and lighting; A is the most efficient with the lowest bills.

questionText: Using notes and freehand sketches, discuss the importance of providing for any two of the following in the design of a house, to enhance the health and wellbeing of the occupants: internal air quality; thermal environment; social interaction.

rows.verbatim: How each could be incorporated to enhance health and wellbeing
rows.contextNote: Any two of the three, each notes 5 and sketches 5 = 10. Internal air quality: natural ventilation through openable glazing; mechanical ventilation with heat recovery supplying filtered fresh air and recovering about 95% of the heat from stale, moist air. Thermal environment: high-quality insulation and high-performance glazing; solar gain from the south, east and west with overhangs, brise-soleil or deciduous trees against overheating; 20 °C in living and 18 °C in sleeping areas. Social interaction: multifunctional rooms such as a table in the kitchen; seating in shared spaces; quieter separate spaces; open plan that can be closed off with pocket doors; outdoor living spaces.

stem: The proposed external wall design detail for a new house is a 215 mm single leaf wall of solid block construction with external insulation, as shown.
questionText: Using the U-value of the wall obtained at 5(a) above and the following data, calculate the cost of heat lost annually through this wall: area of external wall 144 m2; average internal temperature 20 ⁰C; average external temperature 5 ⁰C; heating period 10 hours daily for 37 weeks per annum; cost of oil 97 cent per litre; calorific value of oil 37350 kJ per litre; 1000 watts: 1 kJ per second.

rows.contextNote: Heat loss = U-value × area × temperature difference = 0.191 × 144 × (20 − 5) = 413.068 watts (joules per second).
Heating period = 60 × 60 × 7 × 10 × 37 = 9,324,000 seconds (2,590 hours).

rows.verbatim: Litres of oil for one year

rows.contextNote: Annual cost = 103.118 × €0.97 = €100.02. The scheme’s alternative one-line method gives the same €100.02.

rows.verbatim: Resistance for U- value for 0.12 W/m2 °c (using R=1/U)
rows.contextNote: Required resistance = 1 ÷ 0.12 = 8.333 m²°C/W.

rows.verbatim: Resistance from calculated U-value from part (a)
rows.contextNote: Resistance of the wall from (a) = 1 ÷ 0.191 = 5.229 m²°C/W.
Difference = 8.333 − 5.229 = 3.104 m²°C/W.

rows.contextNote: Additional insulation = 96 mm (95 or 97 mm accepted). Alternative calculation methods are acceptable.

questionText: Explain, with the aid of notes and freehand sketches, any five of the following: strip foundation; fascia board; airtight tape; wind turbine; septic tank; dovetail joint; wall tie; cordless jigsaw; underfloor heating.

rows.contextNote: Explain any five of the nine terms. Each term is marked separately: primary communication of relevant information 6 and other communication 4, in notes or sketches (the scheme reserves no fixed split between them). Strip foundation: a simple, common foundation for homes; concrete reinforced with steel for tensile strength; the wall placed centrally with loads spread at 45° to the ground; used where the soil has a good bearing capacity. Fascia board: gives a finished appearance and protects the house from the weather; part of the eaves with the soffit; carries the gutters; usually wood, PVC or aluminium. Airtight tape: a highly adhesive tape used with an airtight membrane at every junction of building elements and around door and window frames, preventing draughts and heat loss. Wind turbine: converts wind energy into mechanical energy that generates electricity; sustainable, reducing reliance on fossil fuels; commercial wind farms or smaller domestic turbines; horizontal- or vertical-axis. Septic tank: an underground chamber that collects, stores and treats domestic wastewater; anaerobic bacteria break down solids, which settle as sludge; treated water returns to the ground through the percolation area. Dovetail joint: a common joint in drawer and box construction and quality furniture; the slope of the tail (1:8 hardwood, 1:6 softwood) gives its tensile strength; cut by hand or with a router jig. Wall tie: ties the two leaves of a cavity wall into one stable unit, embedded in the mortar; stainless steel or basalt fibre (less thermal bridging); lengths to suit the cavity. Cordless jigsaw: cuts shapes and curves with a reciprocating blade; battery powered, portable and safer without a lead; the base rests on the work and is pushed along; used on a range of materials. Underfloor heating: polyethylene pipes beneath the floor carry water heated by a heat pump; the floor becomes a large heat source with no cold spots and a constant temperature, replacing radiators; efficient at low temperatures.

questionText: Using notes and freehand sketches, discuss the importance of any two of the following in Passive House design: foundation design; solar shading; thermally efficient building envelope.

rows.verbatim: Discuss two Passive House design features
rows.contextNote: Any two of the three, each notes 5 and sketches 5 = 10. Foundation design: highly insulated to a U-value of 0.10–0.15 W/m²K; no thermal bridge at the wall-floor junction; aerated concrete blocks at critical junctions; insulation with high compressive strength; an insulated Passive raft-type foundation. Solar shading: prevents overheating by admitting low winter sun and blocking high summer sun; overhangs or deeper eaves; fixed or adjustable brise-soleil, external blinds, awnings and sliding screens; trees and climbing plants. Thermally efficient building envelope: an unbroken line of insulation and airtightness around the whole building, with every element at its optimum performance; a constant, predictable internal temperature; lower energy use, costs and carbon.

questionText: Explain, with the aid of notes and freehand sketches, any five of the following: concrete mixer; smart radiator valve; ridge tile; triple glazing; balusters; cedar cladding; bridle joint; wood pellet stove; floor screed.

rows.contextNote: Explain any five of the nine terms. Each term is marked separately: primary communication of relevant information 6 and other communication 4, in notes or sketches (the scheme reserves no fixed split between them). Concrete mixer: a rotating drum that turns raw materials into concrete without segregation; small on-site batch mixers (electric, petrol or diesel) are hand loaded and make up to 200 litres per batch, so quality control is difficult; larger quantities come from a mixing plant in a ready-mix truck of 4–6 cubic metres, better regulated and poured directly into the work area. Smart radiator valve: fitted to new or existing radiators; integrated sensors measure the room temperature and signal to reduce or increase the flow of hot water; controlled from smart devices when the owners are away; each room can have its own temperature; reduces energy cost and use. Ridge tile: sits on the apex of the roof and seals the intersection of the two roof planes; traditionally bedded in mortar, now often fixed with integrated dry-fix systems; made from materials like the roof covering, in a variety of colours and profiles. Triple glazing: three panes of glass with cavities usually filled with an inert gas (argon, xenon or krypton); reduces noise and insulates better than double glazing; heavier and thicker, so it may not suit all frames; it can reduce solar gain, so some owners avoid it on the southern elevation. Balusters: vertical members between the handrail and string of a stairs, also called spindles; moulded, square or lathe-turned; must not let a 100 mm diameter sphere pass between them; made of wood, iron or plastic. Cedar cladding: naturally durable, lasting over 60 years without preservative treatment, which is only needed to avoid the weathered silver-grey colour; fixed horizontally or vertically to battens with stainless steel or galvanised fixings, as cedar reacts with ferrous metals; low embodied energy. Bridle joint: a common, strong woodworking joint with a large gluing area; a tee or corner bridle, removing one third of the material from one piece and two thirds from the other; used in frame construction and to join table rails to uprights. Wood pellet stove: heats a home by burning renewable pellets of compressed sawdust and waste wood; an auger feeds fuel steadily from a hopper for a constant flame needing little adjustment; a low-cost heating alternative with very low emissions and a smaller environmental impact. Floor screed: the final layer of the floor on which a floor finish is laid; traditionally sand and cement at 3:1 to 5:1, levelled with a tamping board; modern free-flowing calcium sulphate screeds self-level and suit underfloor heating, at 50–75 mm over pipes clipped to the rigid insulation.

stem: The sketch shows a bungalow which has been retrofitted. The owners have engaged skilled labour in the upgrade of their bungalow to meet the EnerPHit Passive House design standard.
questionText: Using notes and freehand sketches, discuss the importance of any two of the following when carrying out a retrofit to achieve the EnerPHit Passive House design standard: airtightness; windows; building fabric.

rows.verbatim: Discuss the importance of any two in EnerPHit design standard
rows.contextNote: Any two of the three, each notes 6 and sketches 6 = 12. EnerPHit is reached through the five Passive House principles (insulation, limited thermal bridging, triple glazing, airtightness, MVHR), modelled in the PHPP design tool; its space heating demand limit is 25 kWh/m² per year (Passive House 15). Airtightness: Air leakage prevented with airtightness membranes, airtight boards and tapes in timber frame and roofs, and a sand-cement scratch coat, plaster and airtightness paint in block walls; checks for leakage at each stage and a full airtightness test at the end; the EnerPHit target is under 1.0 air changes per hour at 50 Pascals (Passive House 0.6); without airtightness the insulation cannot perform. Windows: Passive House triple-glazed windows of 0.80 W/m²K or less (EnerPHit, installed, 0.85 W/m²K or less); frames in line with the external insulation to avoid a thermal bridge; shading and ventilation planned against summer overheating. Building fabric: Insulation increased to roof, floor and walls (U-value 0.120 W/m²K or less for EnerPHit) by cavity, external or internal insulation; quality workmanship to avoid thermal bridges; external insulation continued below ground level; airtightness and insulation achieved together.

questionText: Explain, with the aid of notes and freehand sketches, any five of the following: site planning notice; halving joint; faceplate turning; smart lighting; cordless drill; plywood; gulley trap; cavity closer; heat pump.

rows.contextNote: Explain any five of the nine terms. Each term is marked separately: primary communication of relevant information 6 and other communication 4, in notes or sketches (the scheme reserves no fixed split between them). Site planning notice: a public notice the applicant erects at the site when applying for planning permission, clearly visible and legible from the road, giving the applicant’s name, site address, type of application and nature of the development; required by planning regulations so the public can make observations or objections; in place for the first five weeks after lodgement, or the application may be invalid. Halving joint: a common, strong woodworking joint with a medium gluing area, made by removing half the material from each piece at the joint; cross, corner, T- or dovetail halving; used in framing and furniture. Faceplate turning: a woodturning method for large, flat circular items such as bowls and plates; the work piece is mounted on a faceplate on the headstock of the lathe; the tool rest supports the chisel; start slowly until the piece is balanced, then increase the speed. Smart lighting: lighting controlled remotely, often automatically, through a smartphone, tablet or voice commands over the internet; scheduling and timers; customised colour, brightness and ambiance; contributes to energy savings. Cordless drill: a portable power tool for drilling holes and driving screws, powered by rechargeable (usually lithium-ion) batteries; more convenient and versatile than a corded drill and usable where there is no power source; features such as an LED light and battery indicator. Plywood: an engineered panel of thin wood veneers glued with the grain of each layer perpendicular to the next for strength; used in construction, furniture and cabinet-making; a strong, relatively low-cost alternative to solid wood; marine plywood for high-moisture use. Gulley trap: a fitting in foul and rainwater drainage with a U-bend that holds water as a seal against sewer gases and odours entering the building; typically underground; needs regular maintenance. Cavity closer: closes the gap between the leaves of a cavity wall at wallplate level and around window and door openings; prevents thermal bridging, damp penetration, air infiltration and condensation; insulating foam or rigid board, 100–150 mm wide to suit the cavity. Heat pump: a device transferring heat from the air, water or ground into the home, distributed by underfloor heating or radiators; runs on electricity with a coefficient of performance of about 3–4; grants encourage the change from fossil-fuel heating.

questionText: Discuss in detail the importance of any two of the following in maintaining a positive health and safety culture among workers on a construction site: safety training; health and safety officer; risk assessment audit.

rows.verbatim: The importance of any two in maintaining a positive health and safety culture
rows.contextNote: Any two of the three, 6 each, discussing why each matters to a positive health and safety culture. Safety training: Safe Pass is mandatory and kept current through refresher courses; training builds awareness of site risks and the skills to identify them and follow best practice; specialist tickets for machinery and vehicles; monitoring and enforcing safe work practices; it may be a condition of the insurance provider. Health and safety officer: provides induction and ongoing training (working at heights, machinery use); develops emergency response plans; keeps first aid and emergency equipment available; ensures the correct PPE is worn; carries out safety inspections and risk assessments; reviews the safety statement; investigates, records and reports accidents. Risk assessment audit: provides a safe working environment; evaluates compliance with safety regulations and policies; identifies hazards and puts control measures in place where a risk cannot be eliminated (for fire: alarms, evacuation signage, drills, extinguishers); recommends improvements; identifies training needs; reduces accidents and liability.

Note 3 and sketch 3. Such as: a safety harness or other fall protection; scaffolding around the stack erected by certified personnel, tied to the house or chimney, with safety rails and toe boards.

stem: The sketch shows the proposed design of a Passive House which is to be constructed in a rural setting.
questionText: Using notes and freehand sketches, discuss the importance of any two of the following in Passive House design: building form; foundation design; space heating energy demand.

rows.verbatim: Discuss the importance of any two in Passive House design
rows.contextNote: Any two of the three, each notes 5 and sketches 5 = 10. Building form: a compact, simple rectangular form with the smallest surface area (A/V ratio 0.7 or less) to cut heat loss, materials and cost; a narrow plan, one room deep, to maximise solar gain; clean lines in walls and roof that make airtightness easy. Foundation design: insulated ring-beam or passive raft foundations wrapped in insulation to eliminate thermal bridging; thermal blocks in the inner-leaf rising wall; 50–100 mm edge insulation at the floor/wall junction; thermally broken wall ties; a U-value of 0.10–0.15 W/m²K. Space heating energy demand: passive house space-heating demand of no more than 15 kWh/m² per year; quality workmanship in airtightness and insulation; eliminating thermal bridges; solar gain through well-designed fenestration; solar shading, thermal mass and controlled ventilation to keep about 20 °C all year.

stem: The external wall of a house built in the 1970s is of single leaf hollow-block construction with an external render. Insulated plasterboard is fixed to the internal surface of the wall. It is proposed to upgrade the thermal properties of the external wall by installing external insulation as shown.
questionText: It has been decided that the wall at 5(a) above should meet the Passive House standard, by further increasing the thickness of the external insulation. Calculate the thickness of additional external insulation required to achieve a U-value of 0.11 W/m2 ºC.

rows.verbatim: Resistance for U-value for 0.11 W/m2 °C (using R=1/U)
rows.contextNote: Required resistance = 1 ÷ 0.11 = 9.091 m²K/W (the scheme first finds R = 1 ÷ 0.221 = 4.525 for the wall at 5(a)).
Additional resistance = 9.091 − 4.525 = 4.566 m²K/W.
R = T ÷ k for the external insulation: 4.566 = T ÷ 0.030.
T = 4.566 × 0.030 = 0.137 m, so 137 mm of additional insulation. Alternative calculation methods are acceptable.

stem: The drawing shows the ground floor plan of a two-storey semi-detached house and a portion of the rear garden. The external walls of the house are 400 mm concrete block walls with a full-fill insulated cavity. The rear wall M-M is south facing. The owners need an additional space for use as a study and occasionally as a family space. The space is to have internal dimensions of 5.0 metres × 3.0 metres as shown. The following options are being considered: (i) building a single-storey extension onto the rear of the house at A. or (ii) building a detached, free-standing space in the garden at B.
questionText: Discuss in detail two advantages and two disadvantages of each option listed at (i) and (ii) above. — Option A

rows.contextNote: An advantage of the single-storey extension at A, discussed for this house (3). Such as: saves on construction and insulation costs; conserves space in the rear garden; more efficient energy use, as it minimises the area of external walling; more freedom in using and dividing the total living space.

A second, different advantage of the extension at A (3). Such as: easy, economical connection to existing services (space heating, plumbing, ventilation, electrical distribution); a compact plan that supports regular social interaction across the generations of the family.

A disadvantage of the extension at A (3). Such as: disturbs the well-proportioned original layout; creates a large undifferentiated space that needs careful design; can reduce the natural lighting and ventilation of the kitchen/dining room; more energy for lighting and heating a large space.

A second, different disadvantage of the extension at A (3). Such as: fewer discrete rooms for a quieter environment; may spoil the view from the existing kitchen and dining area; continuity of insulation and weatherproofing at the roof and wall abutment; spanning the larger opening in the existing external wall may need strengthening and RSJs; misses the chance to connect the garden with the living spaces.

The following options are being considered: (i) building a single-storey extension onto the rear of the house at A. or (ii) building a detached, free-standing space in the garden at B.
questionText: Discuss in detail two advantages and two disadvantages of each option listed at (i) and (ii) above. — Option B

rows.contextNote: An advantage of the detached, free-standing space at B, discussed for this house (3). Such as: keeps the existing relationship between the kitchen/dining area and the outside; minimises disruption during construction; maintains natural lighting to the existing rooms; greater privacy in a distinct room in the garden.

A second, different advantage of the space at B (3). Such as: space for a young or older family member; more freedom of design and more natural lighting in the new building; a closer link between room and garden; isolation for activities that need quiet or are noisy; does not overshadow the existing kitchen and dining room.

A disadvantage of the space at B (3). Such as: a larger external envelope with higher insulation costs; the inconvenience of crossing the garden to reach it; possibly higher heating costs from an extra external door and reduced airtightness.

A second, different disadvantage of the space at B (3). Such as: garden space lost to paths; unusable spaces near the external doors; fragmentation of family living space; the cost of access for all and of connecting services (heating, plumbing and waste, electrical). The scheme prints this list under the heading 3(b)(ii); it belongs to part (a), option B.

questionText:
Using the following data, calculate the U-value of the external wall of a new dwelling house. The wall is of concrete block construction, with a 250 mm cavity. The cavity is a full-fill insulated cavity, with polystyrene bead insulation as shown.
Specification of external wall: external render thickness 16 mm; concrete block outer leaf thickness 100 mm; cavity width 250 mm; concrete block inner leaf thickness 100 mm; internal plaster thickness 12 mm.
Thermal data of external wall: resistance of external surface (R) 0.048 m² °C/W; conductivity of external render (k) 0.720 W/m °C; conductivity of concrete blocks (k) 1.440 W/m °C; conductivity of polystyrene bead (k) 0.031 W/m °C; conductivity of internal plaster (k) 0.220 W/m °C; resistance of internal surface (R) 0.122 m² °C/W.

rows.contextNote: Use a clear resistance table or equivalent method. Convert layer thicknesses from mm to m; R = thickness/conductivity, add both surface resistances and all five material layers, then U = 1/Rtotal. The rubric heading “Insulated concrete ground floor” is a source error: the paper and the worked solution describe the specified external wall.

Seven resistances, 3 each: the five material layers by R = thickness/conductivity, with thicknesses converted from mm to m, and the two given surface resistances. External surface Rse = 0.048 (given; do not divide it by a thickness); external render 0.016/0.720 = 0.02222222; outer concrete-block leaf 0.100/1.440 = 0.06944444; polystyrene bead 0.250/0.031 = 8.06451613 (the cavity is fully filled, so no separate air-cavity resistance); inner concrete-block leaf 0.100/1.440 = 0.06944444 (both leaves count); internal plaster 0.012/0.220 = 0.05454545; internal surface Rsi = 0.122 (given). All in m²·°C/W.

U = 1/Rtotal = 1/8.45017269 = 0.11834078 W/(m²·°C), approximately 0.1183 W/(m²·°C). The rubric awards 1 mark for the formula alone within this 3-mark criterion, not an additional mark. The remaining criteria stay at their own published 3-mark allocations.

questionText:
Using the U-value obtained at 5(a) and the data given below, calculate the cost of heat lost annually through the external walls of the new house - as specified at 5(a) above.
Data for both houses: area of external wall of each house 150 m²; average internal temperature 20 °C; average external temperature 6 °C; heating period 8 hours per day, every day for 35 weeks per annum; cost of oil 95 cent per litre; calorific value of oil 37350 kJ per litre; 1000 watts: 1kJ per second.

rows.contextNote: Use heat-loss rate = U × A × ΔT, with ΔT = 20 − 6 = 14 °C. For this house, 0.11834078 × 150 × 14 ≈ 248.51563 W (J/s). Use the U-value appropriate to this house; rate alone is not annual energy or cost.

8 × 7 × 35 = 1,960 hours = 7,056,000 seconds. The worked scheme prints “3,157 hours” beside the correct seconds; that parenthetical hours figure is an error. Follow the paper’s schedule and the correct seconds, not 3,157 hours.
Annual wall heat loss = heat-loss rate × 7,056,000 / 1,000 ≈ 1,753,526.29 kJ. The factor 1,000 converts J to kJ; keep watts, seconds and the oil calorific value in consistent units.

rows.verbatim: Litres of oil for one year
rows.contextNote: Litres = annual energy / 37,350 ≈ 46.94850 litres. This uses the calorific value given in the paper; do not invent an unstated boiler-efficiency factor.

Cost = litres × €0.95 ≈ €44.60107. Using unrounded values gives €44.60 to the nearest cent. The scheme also prints €44.58 using a rounded U = 0.1183 and intermediate truncation; calculating directly with that U gives €44.58570 (normally €44.59). Accept coherent rounding consistent with the working rather than demanding the source’s truncation. Alternative direct or proportional methods may earn the equivalent published criteria; do not award the same calculation twice.

questionText:
(a) Using the following data, calculate the U-value of the external wall of a new dwelling house. The wall is of concrete block construction, with a 250 mm cavity. The cavity is a full-fill insulated cavity, with polystyrene bead insulation as shown.
Specification of external wall: external render thickness 16 mm; concrete block outer leaf thickness 100 mm; cavity width 250 mm; concrete block inner leaf thickness 100 mm; internal plaster thickness 12 mm.
Thermal data of external wall: resistance of external surface (R) 0.048 m² °C/W; conductivity of external render (k) 0.720 W/m °C; conductivity of concrete blocks (k) 1.440 W/m °C; conductivity of polystyrene bead (k) 0.031 W/m °C; conductivity of internal plaster (k) 0.220 W/m °C; resistance of internal surface (R) 0.122 m² °C/W.

(b) Using the U-value obtained at 5(a) and the data given below, calculate the cost of heat lost annually through the external walls of each of the following: the new house - as specified at 5(a) above and an existing house that complies with current Building Regulations, having a U-value of 0.21 W/m² °C for the walls.
Data for both houses: area of external wall of each house 150 m²; average internal temperature 20 °C; average external temperature 6 °C; heating period 8 hours per day, every day for 35 weeks per annum; cost of oil 95 cent per litre; calorific value of oil 37350 kJ per litre; 1000 watts: 1kJ per second.

(c) Using notes and freehand sketches, show best practice design detailing to prevent the ingress of water at the window head in the wall of the new house specified at 5(a) above.

rows.contextNote: Use a clear resistance table or equivalent method. Convert layer thicknesses from mm to m; R = thickness/conductivity, add both surface resistances and all five material layers, then U = 1/Rtotal. The rubric heading “Insulated concrete ground floor” is a source error: the paper and the worked solution describe the specified external wall.

Seven resistances, 3 each: the five material layers by R = thickness/conductivity, with thicknesses converted from mm to m, and the two given surface resistances. External surface Rse = 0.048 (given; do not divide it by a thickness); external render 0.016/0.720 = 0.02222222; outer concrete-block leaf 0.100/1.440 = 0.06944444; polystyrene bead 0.250/0.031 = 8.06451613 (the cavity is fully filled, so no separate air-cavity resistance); inner concrete-block leaf 0.100/1.440 = 0.06944444 (both leaves count); internal plaster 0.012/0.220 = 0.05454545; internal surface Rsi = 0.122 (given). All in m²·°C/W.

U = 1/Rtotal = 1/8.45017269 = 0.11834078 W/(m²·°C), approximately 0.1183 W/(m²·°C). The rubric awards 1 mark for the formula alone within this 3-mark criterion, not an additional mark. The remaining criteria stay at their own published 3-mark allocations.

Annual wall heat loss = heat-loss rate × 7,056,000 / 1,000 ≈ 1,753,526.29 kJ. The factor 1,000 converts J to kJ; keep watts, seconds and the oil calorific value in consistent units.

rows.contextNote: For this distinct design feature, award notes 5 and a relevant freehand sketch 5. questionText: Discuss in detail the importance of designing nearly zero energy buildings (NZEB) for the 21st century.

rows.verbatim: Discussion of NZEB design for 21st century
rows.contextNote: Award 4 marks for a relevant point and 6 for its developed discussion, total 10. Explain why very low energy demand, high energy performance and appropriate renewable supply matter for long-term resource use, climate impact, energy costs/security or fair access to resources. The scheme describes very high energy performance with the small remaining demand met to a significant extent by renewables on-site or nearby; NZEB does not require every building to be off-grid. stem: The roof of a new house, as shown, is a traditional cut roof and has a pitch of 45 degrees. The house has an internal width of 6.0 metres and the roof is highly insulated. Insulated plasterboard is also fixed to the underside of the rafters and is finished with a plaster skim coat. The external wall supporting the floor joists is a 400 mm concrete block wall with a full-fill insulated cavity. The 225 mm × 40 mm floor joists are supported centrally on a 100 mm internal load-bearing concrete block wall. The attic floor is finished with 25 mm tongue-and-groove floor boards.
questionText: To a scale of 1:10, draw a vertical section through one half of the roof structure from eaves up to ridge, showing one external wall and one rafter length. stem: Light is what architecture is all about. It is as fundamental for the soul as air, fire, earth and water. Light has been one of the key elements of architecture since the Modern movement began (and glass technology improved) at the turn of the 20th century. Yet, light has traditionally been lacking in Irish homes. Many old cottages only have windows on the south side and none on the north. Now glass has improved and windows can be made with incredibly low U-values (meaning it doesn’t let the cold through), so you can now have large glazed areas without heat loss. We need light and instinctively search for it. People move to the part of the room where there is natural light and children instinctively play in pools of light. Adapted from LOVE YOUR HOME Secrets to a Successful Space by Dermot Bannon (2014) Published by Gill & Macmillan. ISBN: 978 07171 6448 6

questionRef: 2015 OL Q2(a) — filling the cavity with insulation
stem: The sketch shows a dwelling house which was built over 40 years ago. The external wall is a 300 mm concrete block wall with a 100 mm cavity. There is no insulation in the cavity. It is proposed to insulate the external wall by: filling the cavity with insulation and adding an external system of insulation to the wall.
questionText: It is proposed to insulate the external wall by: filling the cavity with insulation. Using notes and freehand sketches, show the steps to be followed in applying each system of insulation to the wall.

rows.verbatim: Filling the cavity with insulation – Notes
rows.contextNote: Three valid steps, 4 marks each. Typical procedure (carried out by specialist firms): 22 mm diameter holes are drilled through the external leaf, usually spaced about 800 mm horizontally and 1350 mm vertically; special care is taken at damp proof courses and at heads of windows and doors, with extra holes drilled around openings so the cavity fills properly; polystyrene beads are pumped into the cavity while a light coating of glue is applied, setting into a solid structure; when pumping is complete the holes are filled. Other valid steps are acceptable.

rows.verbatim: Filling the cavity with insulation – Sketches
rows.contextNote: Quality of sketches for the cavity-fill steps: excellent 8, good 6, fair 4. The scheme sketches show the drill entering the outer leaf and the hole spacing on the wall.

stem: The sketch shows a dwelling house which was built over 40 years ago. The external wall is a 300 mm concrete block wall with a 100 mm cavity. There is no insulation in the cavity. questionText: It is proposed to insulate the external wall by: adding an external system of insulation to the wall. Using notes and freehand sketches, show the steps to be followed in applying each system of insulation to the wall.

rows.verbatim: Adding an external system of insulation to the wall – Notes
rows.contextNote: Three valid steps, 4 marks each. Typical procedure: the first row of insulation boards is fixed in place resting on a stainless steel track; boards are fixed in position with a special adhesive, and all rows are fixed and the adhesive allowed to set; mechanical fixings (typically about seven per square metre, longer for thicker boards) are installed by drilling through the insulation into the wall and then hammered into place. Typical insulation materials: polystyrene, mineral fibre board, wood fibre board. Other valid steps are acceptable.

stem: The sketch shows a dwelling house which was built over 40 years ago. The external wall is a 300 mm concrete block wall with a 100 mm cavity. There is no insulation in the cavity. It is proposed to insulate the external wall by: filling the cavity with insulation and adding an external system of insulation to the wall.
questionText: Using notes and freehand sketches, show the steps to be followed in applying each system of insulation to the wall.

rows.verbatim: Filling the cavity with insulation – Notes
rows.contextNote: Three valid steps, 4 marks each. Typical procedure (carried out by specialist firms): 22 mm diameter holes are drilled through the external leaf, usually spaced about 800 mm horizontally and 1350 mm vertically; special care is taken at damp proof courses and at heads of windows and doors, with extra holes drilled around openings so the cavity fills properly; polystyrene beads are pumped into the cavity while a light coating of glue is applied, setting into a solid structure; when pumping is complete the holes are filled. Other valid steps are acceptable.

rows.verbatim: Filling the cavity with insulation – Sketches
rows.contextNote: Quality of sketches for the cavity-fill steps: excellent 8, good 6, fair 4. The scheme sketches show the drill entering the outer leaf and the hole spacing on the wall.

rows.verbatim: Adding an external system of insulation to the wall – Notes
rows.contextNote: Three valid steps, 4 marks each. Typical procedure: the first row of insulation boards is fixed in place resting on a stainless steel track; boards are fixed in position with a special adhesive, and all rows are fixed and the adhesive allowed to set; mechanical fixings (typically about seven per square metre, longer for thicker boards) are installed by drilling through the insulation into the wall and then hammered into place. Typical insulation materials: polystyrene, mineral fibre board, wood fibre board. Other valid steps are acceptable.

stem: The sketch shows a dwelling house with a traditional slated cut roof. The roof has a pitch of 30° and is highly insulated at ceiling joist level. The internal span of the house is 5.8 metres. The walls of the house are of 450 mm rendered concrete block construction with a full-fill insulated cavity.
questionText: To a scale of 1:10, draw a vertical section through one half of the roof structure, from just below eaves up to the ridge. Show one external wall and one rafter length. Include the typical construction details from 600 mm below the ceiling joists up to the ridge, and include three courses of slate at eaves. Include four typical dimensions.

rows.contextNote: Three external-wall details, 4 each (3 for drawing, 1 for annotation). Typical: external and internal render; 100 mm external and internal block leaves; wall ties; 250 mm full-fill insulated cavity; cavity closer; 100 mm × 75 mm wallplate(s).

Four roof-structure details, 4 each (3 drawing, 1 annotation). Typical: 200 mm × 50 mm rafters at 400 mm centres; ceiling joists at 400 mm centres; 225 mm × 75 mm purlin; strut supporting the purlin; hanger; collar tie at each couple or at 1200 mm centres; ridge board; plasterboard with 350 mm insulation laid in three layers.

Four eaves details, 4 each (3 drawing, 1 annotation). Typical: tilting fillet; fascia board, soffit and gutter (any two); 25 mm fascia ventilator and 50 mm proprietary eaves ventilator; wind-tightness barrier; breather membrane laid over the rafters; 50 mm × 30 mm slating battens; three courses of slates.
Four appropriate typical dimensions on the section.
Scale 4 and drafting 4, assessed together: excellent 8, good 6, fair 4.

stem: Lifetime use of a dwelling should be a key consideration at the design stage.
questionText: Using notes and freehand sketches, discuss two best-practice guidelines that should be followed when designing for lifetime use at each of the following areas of a dwelling: entrance access.

rows.contextNote: First guideline for the entrance access: notes 4 and sketches 4. Such as: a level threshold (maximum 15 mm upstand, chamfered or rounded edges) with a recessed drainage channel and the internal floor flush; a 1000 mm minimum clear door opening; a slip-resistant approach path at 1:20 or flatter (ramps no steeper than 1:12, with level landings); a level landing of at least 1500 mm × 1500 mm outside the door and 300 mm clear space at the leading edge; a canopy or recess at least 900 mm deep; lever handles 800–1050 mm above floor level and low door-closer force; a vision panel; motion-sensor lighting.
Second, different guideline for the entrance access: notes 4 and sketches 4. Do not credit the same guideline twice.

stem: Lifetime use of a dwelling should be a key consideration at the design stage.
questionText:
(a) Using notes and freehand sketches, discuss two best-practice guidelines that should be followed when designing for lifetime use at each of the following areas of a dwelling: entrance access; bathroom.

(b) The drawing shows the ground floor plan of a draft design for an adjoining garage conversion. The homeowner wishes to convert the garage, so that a family member with reduced mobility can live independently. With reference to the design shown, using notes and freehand sketches, discuss three specific design considerations for the open-plan kitchen/dining and living area, that ensures ease of use by a person with reduced mobility. Indicate on your sketches, typical dimensions as appropriate.

(c) Discuss in detail two reasons why it is important to consider lifetime use at the design stage of a dwelling.

rows.contextNote: First guideline for the entrance access: notes 4 and sketches 4. Such as: a level threshold (maximum 15 mm upstand, chamfered or rounded edges) with a recessed drainage channel and the internal floor flush; a 1000 mm minimum clear door opening; a slip-resistant approach path at 1:20 or flatter (ramps no steeper than 1:12, with level landings); a level landing of at least 1500 mm × 1500 mm outside the door and 300 mm clear space at the leading edge; a canopy or recess at least 900 mm deep; lever handles 800–1050 mm above floor level and low door-closer force; a vision panel; motion-sensor lighting.
Second, different guideline for the entrance access: notes 4 and sketches 4. Do not credit the same guideline twice.

First guideline for the bathroom: notes 4 and sketches 4. Such as: an accessible bathroom on the entry level; a clear turning circle of at least Ø1500 mm (ideally Ø1800 mm); walls reinforced with 18 mm plywood or noggins for future grab rails; a level-access (wet-room) shower graded to a gully; a door opening outwards or sliding with at least 800 mm clear opening; a WC 450–480 mm high and a wall-hung basin; lever taps; large rocker switches or pull cords 900–1200 mm above floor level; slip-resistant flooring.
Second, different guideline for the bathroom: notes 4 and sketches 4. Do not credit the same guideline twice.
Notes 3 and sketches 3, related to the plan shown. Such as: Ø1500 mm (ideally Ø1800 mm) turning circles and 1200 mm clear routes between furniture and units.

Notes 3 and sketches 3. Such as: worktops lowered to 760–820 mm with knee space (minimum 700 mm high × 600 mm deep) under the sink and hob; pull-out or pull-down storage within the 400–1200 mm reach zone.

Notes 3 and sketches 3. Such as: dining table with 1200 mm clearance and 700 mm clear underside; firm slip-resistant level floors (transitions no more than 5 mm); level threshold to the folding doors; sockets at least 400 mm and switches/thermostats no higher than 1200 mm. Three distinct considerations are needed.
Two appropriate typical dimensions shown on the sketches.
Point 2 and discussion 2. Such as: future-proofing so occupants can age in place; accessible features are far cheaper built in than retrofitted.

A second, different reason: point 2 and discussion 2. Such as: inclusivity for visitors and families with young children; fewer trips and falls; an adaptable house lasts longer and needs less new construction; wider market appeal and resale value.

stem: Shown in the sketch is the proposed external wall design detail for a new house of timber frame construction.
questionText: Calculate the U-value of the proposed wall, given the construction has the following sequence and data: External render thickness 16 mm External concrete block thickness 100 mm Clear cavity width 60 mm Oriented Strand Board (OSB) thickness 12 mm Timber stud thickness 250 mm Insulation between studs thickness 250 mm Oriented Strand Board (OSB) thickness 12 mm Plasterboard thickness 12.5 mm. Thermal data of the external wall: Resistance of external surface (R) 0.048 m2 ºC/W; Resistivity of external render (r) 2.170 m ºC/W; Conductivity of concrete block (k) 1.440 W/m ºC; Resistance of clear cavity (R) 0.440 m2 ºC/W; Conductivity of OSB (k) 0.130 W/m ºC; Conductivity of insulation (k) 0.039 W/m ºC; Conductivity of OSB (k) 0.130 W/m ºC; Conductivity of plasterboard (k) 0.250 W/m ºC; Resistance of internal surface (R) 0.130 m2 ºC/W. Note: The timber studs need not be considered in your calculations.

rows.contextNote: Set out the layers, thicknesses (in metres), k or r values and resistances in a table.
External surface resistance 0.048 and internal surface resistance 0.130 m²°C/W, 3 each.

Seven layer resistances, 3 each: render 0.016 × 2.170 = 0.035; concrete block 0.100 ÷ 1.440 = 0.069; clear cavity 0.440 (given); OSB 0.012 ÷ 0.130 = 0.092; insulation 0.250 ÷ 0.039 = 6.410; OSB 0.092; plasterboard 0.0125 ÷ 0.250 = 0.050 m²°C/W. The studs are ignored, as the question states.
Total resistance Rt = 7.367 m²°C/W (sum of all resistances).
U = 1 ÷ Rt = 1 ÷ 7.367 = 0.136 W/m²°C, with units.

sourceMaterial.attribution: SEC Leaving Certificate Construction Studies 2026 Higher Level — © State Examinations Commission.
sourceMaterial.presentationNote: All printed data are retained in the original question. Part (b) uses the U-value from part (a); the scheme’s worked answers are U = 0.136 W/m²°C and an annual cost of €40.27.

stem: Shown in the sketch is the proposed external wall design detail for a new house of timber frame construction.
questionText: Using the U-value of the wall obtained at 5(a) above and the following data, calculate the cost of heat lost annually through this wall: area of external wall 144 m2; average internal temperature 20 ºC; average external temperature 7 ºC; heating period 6 hours daily for 33 weeks per annum; cost of wood pellets 55 cent per kg; calorific value of wood pellets 17350 kJ per kg; 1000 watts 1 kJ per second.

rows.contextNote: Heat loss = U × area × temperature difference = 0.136 × 144 × (20 − 7) = 254.592 W (J/s).
Heating time = 60 × 60 × 6 × 7 × 33 = 4,989,600 seconds per year.

rows.verbatim: Kgs of wood pellets for one year
rows.contextNote: Wood pellets = 1,270,312.243 ÷ 17,350 = 73.2168 kg per year.
Cost = 73.2168 × €0.55 = €40.27 per year. The single-formula method (U × area × ΔT × seconds × cost ÷ (calorific value × 1000)) gives the same €40.27.

stem: “It would be reasonable to assume that ensuring good indoor air quality would be a key factor when designing and constructing buildings. The term sick building syndrome became well known in the 1980’s and still lingers today, though largely associated with poorly air-conditioned offices. However, the health impacts of buildings are still poorly understood and rarely taken into account as a key priority when buildings are designed or renovated. Architects, when specifying building materials are mainly concerned with cost, availability, robustness and aesthetics, not their impacts on health.” Adapted from: Building Materials, Health and Indoor Air Quality: No Breathing Space by Tom Wooley
questionText: Discuss the above statement in detail.

rows.contextNote: Point 5 and discussion 5. Such as: people spend most of their lives indoors, yet health is often overlooked behind cost, appearance, durability and availability; sick building syndrome symptoms linked to poor ventilation, mould and chemical emissions.

Point 5 and discussion 5. Such as: more airtight buildings need carefully designed ventilation; VOCs and formaldehyde from paints, adhesives, finishes and composite boards; condensation and mould from poor detailing, especially in Ireland’s damp climate.

Point 5 and discussion 5. Such as: health impacts are harder to measure and appear later, while healthier materials can cost more; Passive House/EnerPHit ventilation with heat recovery, low-VOC materials, daylight and newer certification standards show a growing focus on wellbeing. Three distinct, well-argued points are needed.

stem: A triple glazed window is fitted in the external wall of a dwelling house, as shown. The window has a thermally broken wooden frame. The fixed frame of the window is 120 mm × 80 mm. The wall is of timber frame construction with an external rendered concrete block outer leaf. The internal timber frame is 250 mm × 50 mm with a 50 mm service cavity provided at the internal surface. The bottom of the concrete cill is located 300 mm above finished floor level. The ground floor is a solid concrete floor with a 20 mm quarry tile finish.
questionText:
(a) To a scale of 1:5, draw a vertical section through the external wall, ground floor, and window. Show the typical construction details from the bottom of the strip foundation to a level 200 mm above the bottom frame of the window. Show a 1.0 metre width of ground floor.

(b) On your drawing, show the typical design detailing that will prevent the penetration of radon gas into the house.

rows.verbatim: Foundation and solid concrete ground floor – typical detailing
rows.contextNote: Best five foundation and ground-floor details, 4 each (3 for drawing, 1 for annotation). Marking menu: R.C. strip foundation; dead blockwork and cavity wall above foundation; cavity infill; thermal blocks on inner leaf; DPC; hardcore/sand blinding/radon barrier; subfloor; insulation; screed; airtightness barrier at floor and wall junction; 20 mm quarry tile finish/skirting board.

Best four external-wall details, 4 each (3 for drawing, 1 for annotation). Marking menu: external render; concrete block outer leaf; air space/residual cavity; anchor strap; breather membrane; racking board; 250 × 50 mm stud detail and insulation; OSB sheeting; airtightness membrane; 50 mm insulated service cavity; plasterboard and skim.

Best three window details, 4 each (3 for drawing, 1 for annotation). Marking menu: cavity closer; concrete window cill; DPC at cill (cill wrapped in DPC); thermally broken window frame; window board; triple glazing; airtight barrier at junction.
Scale 4 and drafting 4, assessed together: excellent 8, good 6, fair 4.

rows.verbatim: Design detailing identified to prevent the penetration of radon gas
rows.contextNote: Show and identify the radon barrier: a gas-resistant membrane across the ground floor, carried continuously across the wall as in the scheme’s model detail. Any other relevant point is acceptable.

questionText:
(a) Using notes and freehand sketches, show a revised internal layout for the ground floor that incorporates each of the above design requirements.

(b) Outline three reasons for your proposed layout.

(c) Using notes and freehand sketches, show a revised external design for the garage that will enhance the overall visual appearance of the house.

rows.verbatim: Revised internal layout for the ground floor and garage space
rows.contextNote: Notes and freehand sketch of a coherent revised ground-floor plan that uses the garage space and respects the south-facing wall A-A. Such as (two model layouts): remove the wall between the garage and utility for one large space; replace the garage door with high-performance glazing; a corner window on the south-west; sliding or bi-fold doors to a patio; doorways into the corridor or at both ends of the new space (steel beams where a wall is load-bearing).
A downstairs bathroom included, for example a large family bathroom where the kitchen or dining room was, on an external wall with easy access to the drainage.

rows.verbatim: Create an open-plan kitchen/dining and living area
rows.contextNote: An open-plan kitchen/dining and living area, for example by combining the garage and utility into one large space.

rows.verbatim: Optimising daylight into the ground floor
rows.contextNote: Daylight optimised, for example high-performance glazing on the south and west, a corner window, roof lights in the garage roof, or glazed doors between rooms.

One reason for the layout. Such as: combining the garage and utility gives a large south-facing space for open-plan kitchen/dining and living; high-performance glazing in place of the garage door improves solar gain and thermal performance.

A second reason. Such as: south-facing glazing makes the open-plan space bright and warm and lessens the need for artificial light and energy bills; glazed doors let evening light from the west into the sitting room.

A third reason. Such as: a large, wheelchair-accessible family bathroom suits lifetime use; roof lights flood the new space with light for wellbeing; matching brick keeps the character of the converted garage. Three distinct reasons are needed.

Such as: replace the garage door with high-performance glazing (full height or above worktop level); the same plaster finish as the house, or brick to strengthen the connection with it; glazing to the south and west and roof lights in the garage roof; solar shading against overheating; keep a bitumen flat roof, use zinc, or raise the pitch and slate it to match the house.

stem: The external wall of a house built in the 1970s is of single leaf hollow-block construction with an external render. Insulated plasterboard is fixed to the internal surface of the wall. It is proposed to upgrade the thermal properties of the external wall by installing external insulation as shown.
questionText: Calculate the U-value of the proposed wall, given the construction has the following sequence and data: External acrylic render thickness 8 mm External polystyrene insulation thickness 100 mm External render thickness 16 mm Hollow concrete block thickness 215 mm Insulation thickness 25 mm Plasterboard thickness 12.5 mm Internal skim coat thickness 3 mm. Thermal data of the external wall: Resistance of external surface (R) 0.048 m2 ºC/W; Conductivity of acrylic render (k) 0.670 W/m ºC; Conductivity of external insulation (k) 0.030 W/m ºC; Resistivity of external render (r) 2.170 m ºC/W; Resistance of hollow concrete block (R) 0.210 m2 ºC/W; Conductivity of insulation (k) 0.037 W/m ºC; Conductivity of plasterboard (k) 0.160 W/m ºC; Resistivity of skim coat (r) 5.550 m ºC/W; Resistance of internal surface (R) 0.122 m2 ºC/W.

rows.contextNote: External surface resistance 0.048 m²°C/W (given).
Internal surface resistance 0.122 m²°C/W (given).

Seven layer resistances, 3 each: acrylic render 0.008 ÷ 0.670 = 0.012; external insulation 0.100 ÷ 0.030 = 3.333; sand cement render 0.016 × 2.170 = 0.035; hollow concrete block 0.210 (given); insulation 0.025 ÷ 0.037 = 0.676; plasterboard 0.0125 ÷ 0.160 = 0.078; internal skim coat 0.003 × 5.550 = 0.017 m²°C/W.
Total resistance Rt = 4.531 m²°C/W (sum of all resistances).
U = 1 ÷ Rt = 1 ÷ 4.531 = 0.221 W/m²°C, with units.

sourceMaterial.label: ORIGINAL QUESTION 5
sourceMaterial.title: Externally insulated hollow-block wall: U-value, heat-loss cost and Passive House upgrade
sourceMaterial.attribution: SEC Leaving Certificate Construction Studies 2025 Higher Level — © State Examinations Commission.
sourceMaterial.presentationNote: All printed data are retained in the original question. Parts (b) and (c) use the U-value from part (a); the scheme’s worked answers are U = 0.221 W/m²°C, an annual cost of €76.34 and 137 mm of additional insulation.

stem: The external wall of a house built in the 1970s is of single leaf hollow-block construction with an external render. Insulated plasterboard is fixed to the internal surface of the wall. It is proposed to upgrade the thermal properties of the external wall by installing external insulation as shown.
questionText: Using the U-value of the wall obtained at 5(a) above and the following data, calculate the cost of heat lost annually through this wall: area of external wall 144 m2; average internal temperature 19 ºC; average external temperature 6 ºC; heating period 7 hours daily for 33 weeks per annum; cost of wood pellets 55 cent per kg; calorific value of wood pellets 17350 kJ per kg; 1000 Watts 1 kJ per second.

rows.contextNote: Heat loss = U × area × temperature difference = 0.221 × 144 × (19 − 6) = 413.712 W (J/s).
Heating time = 60 × 60 × 7 × 7 × 33 = 5,821,200 seconds per year (1,344 hours).

rows.verbatim: Kgs of wood pellets for one year
rows.contextNote: Wood pellets = 2,408,300.29 ÷ 17,350 = 138.810 kg per year.
Cost = 138.810 × €0.55 = €76.34 per year. The single-formula method (U × area × ΔT × seconds × cost ÷ (calorific value × 1000)) gives the same €76.34.

stem: The external wall of a house built in the 1970s is of single leaf hollow-block construction with an external render. Insulated plasterboard is fixed to the internal surface of the wall. questionText:
(a) Calculate the U-value of the proposed wall, given the construction has the following sequence and data: External acrylic render thickness 8 mm External polystyrene insulation thickness 100 mm External render thickness 16 mm Hollow concrete block thickness 215 mm Insulation thickness 25 mm Plasterboard thickness 12.5 mm Internal skim coat thickness 3 mm. Thermal data of the external wall: Resistance of external surface (R) 0.048 m2 ºC/W; Conductivity of acrylic render (k) 0.670 W/m ºC; Conductivity of external insulation (k) 0.030 W/m ºC; Resistivity of external render (r) 2.170 m ºC/W; Resistance of hollow concrete block (R) 0.210 m2 ºC/W; Conductivity of insulation (k) 0.037 W/m ºC; Conductivity of plasterboard (k) 0.160 W/m ºC; Resistivity of skim coat (r) 5.550 m ºC/W; Resistance of internal surface (R) 0.122 m2 ºC/W.

(b) Using the U-value of the wall obtained at 5(a) above and the following data, calculate the cost of heat lost annually through this wall: area of external wall 144 m2; average internal temperature 19 ºC; average external temperature 6 ºC; heating period 7 hours daily for 33 weeks per annum; cost of wood pellets 55 cent per kg; calorific value of wood pellets 17350 kJ per kg; 1000 Watts 1 kJ per second.

(c) It has been decided that the wall at 5(a) above should meet the Passive House standard, by further increasing the thickness of the external insulation. Calculate the thickness of additional external insulation required to achieve a U-value of 0.11 W/m2 ºC.

rows.contextNote: External surface resistance 0.048 m²°C/W (given).
Internal surface resistance 0.122 m²°C/W (given).

Seven layer resistances, 3 each: acrylic render 0.008 ÷ 0.670 = 0.012; external insulation 0.100 ÷ 0.030 = 3.333; sand cement render 0.016 × 2.170 = 0.035; hollow concrete block 0.210 (given); insulation 0.025 ÷ 0.037 = 0.676; plasterboard 0.0125 ÷ 0.160 = 0.078; internal skim coat 0.003 × 5.550 = 0.017 m²°C/W.
Total resistance Rt = 4.531 m²°C/W (sum of all resistances).
U = 1 ÷ Rt = 1 ÷ 4.531 = 0.221 W/m²°C, with units.
Heat loss = U × area × temperature difference = 0.221 × 144 × (19 − 6) = 413.712 W (J/s).
Heating time = 60 × 60 × 7 × 7 × 33 = 5,821,200 seconds per year (1,344 hours).

rows.verbatim: Kgs of wood pellets for one year
rows.contextNote: Wood pellets = 2,408,300.29 ÷ 17,350 = 138.810 kg per year.
Cost = 138.810 × €0.55 = €76.34 per year. The single-formula method (U × area × ΔT × seconds × cost ÷ (calorific value × 1000)) gives the same €76.34.

rows.verbatim: Resistance for U-value for 0.11 W/m2 °C (using R=1/U)
rows.contextNote: Required resistance = 1 ÷ 0.11 = 9.091 m²K/W (the scheme first finds R = 1 ÷ 0.221 = 4.525 for the wall at 5(a)).
Additional resistance = 9.091 − 4.525 = 4.566 m²K/W.
R = T ÷ k for the external insulation: 4.566 = T ÷ 0.030.
T = 4.566 × 0.030 = 0.137 m, so 137 mm of additional insulation. Alternative calculation methods are acceptable.
