questionText: Explain, with the aid of notes and freehand sketches, any five of the following: raft foundation; housing joint; rainwater butt; stud wall; laser level; damp-proof course; door threshold; baluster; room thermostat.

rows.contextNote: Explain any five of the nine terms. Each term is marked separately: primary communication of relevant information 6 and other communication 4, in notes or sketches (the scheme reserves no fixed split between them). Raft foundation: a large, continuous reinforced concrete slab supporting the whole structure, "floating" like a raft; spreads the load over the whole footprint, reducing pressure on the soil; suits soils of low bearing capacity; needs more steel and concrete than a strip foundation. Housing joint: a groove or slot cut across the width of one piece receives the end of another; a medium gluing area; used for shelves, cabinets and bookcases; a through housing runs fully across and shows at both ends, a stopped housing hides the joint at the front edge. Rainwater butt: a container that collects and stores rainwater from the roof via gutters and downpipes; reuses water for plants, lawns or washing the car; reduces reliance on treated tap water and lowers metered water use. Stud wall: an internal wall framed with vertical timber or metal studs covered with plasterboard on both sides; lighter and faster to build than a block wall; load-bearing or non-load-bearing; houses electrical and plumbing services; poorer sound insulation and bearing capacity than a block wall. Laser level: a tool projecting a laser beam to give a straight, level reference line, vertical and/or horizontal; a rotary laser projects a 360° beam for large or outdoor work; more accurate than a spirit level; can be mounted on tripods or clamps. Damp-proof course: a barrier stopping moisture rising through walls and floors by capillary action; polythene, bitumen felt, lead or copper, or slate; laid horizontally between courses, typically 150 mm above ground level, and around window and door openings; protects finishes and reduces mould and decay. Door threshold: the strip of wood, metal or plastic at the bottom of a doorway where the door closes; bridges two floor surfaces and seals the doorway; external thresholds keep out weather and draughts; internal ones cover changes in floor level; must meet building regulations so they are not a trip hazard. Baluster: a short vertical post, often decorative, supporting the handrail of a stairs; a row of balusters is a balustrade; a safety element preventing falls, especially by children; also on balconies and terraces; wood, metal, glass or concrete. Room thermostat: controls room temperature by switching the heating on below the set point and off above it; keeps rooms comfortable efficiently; manual dial or digital models; smart thermostats connect to Wi-Fi and a smartphone.

questionText: Explain, with the aid of notes and freehand sketches, any five of the following: triple glazing; wind turbine; carbon monoxide alarm; mortise and tenon joint; butt hinge; ball valve; cordless circular saw; fascia board; smart meter.

rows.contextNote: Explain any five of the nine terms. Each term is marked separately: primary communication of relevant information 6 and other communication 4, in notes or sketches (the scheme reserves no fixed split between them). Triple glazing: three panes of glass separated by insulating gaps, often argon-filled; more energy efficient than single or double glazing; high thermal and sound insulation; typically dearer than double glazing. Wind turbine: converts the kinetic energy of wind into electricity; renewable, emission-free generation; on land or offshore, singly or in wind farms; Ireland produces a large share of its energy from wind. Carbon monoxide alarm: detects carbon monoxide, a colourless, odourless, poisonous gas from fuel-burning appliances (boilers, stoves, fires, heaters), and sounds a warning; mandatory when installing new or replacement fossil-fuel appliances; test it regularly. Mortise and tenon joint: a tenon cut on the end of one piece fits a mortise cut in the other; very strong with a large gluing area; used for chair and table legs and rails, doors and windows; a stopped joint hides the tenon. Butt hinge: a common hinge joining a door to its frame; two rectangular leaves joined by knuckles and a pin; the leaves sit flush when the door closes; for interior or exterior doors, cabinets and lids; strong and affordable. Ball valve: controls flow with a rotating ball with a hole through it; open when the hole lines up with the pipe, closed when it is at right angles; the handle shows open, closed or partly open; used to isolate plumbing for maintenance or emergencies. Cordless circular saw: a portable battery-powered (usually lithium-ion) saw for cutting wood, and sometimes metal or plastic, without a mains cable; can make rip, cross and bevel cuts. Fascia board: a horizontal board fixed to the ends of the rafters along the lower edge of the roof; timber or uPVC; protects the rafter ends and supports the gutter; closes the roof against moisture and pests; available in colours and decorative profiles. Smart meter: an electricity meter that records use automatically and sends readings to the supplier, ending manual and estimated readings; splits use into day, night and peak times; shows usage patterns to help choose a tariff and save energy.

questionText: Explain, with the aid of notes and freehand sketches, any five of the following: box dovetail joint; triple glazing; solar panel; cordless drill; skirting board; compression fitting; natural seasoning; concrete lintel; radon barrier.

rows.contextNote: Explain any five of the nine terms. Each term is marked separately: primary communication of relevant information 6 and other communication 4, in notes or sketches (the scheme reserves no fixed split between them). Box dovetail joint: a joint for box shapes and a common joint in high-quality furniture, made by hand or with special jigs; the slope of the dovetails matters for strength, usually 1:6 in softwood and 1:8 in hardwood; it gives a decorative appearance, sometimes highlighted with contrasting woods. A sketch should show the interlocking tails and pins at the corner. Triple glazing: three panes of glass with a cavity between each; a better insulator and better acoustic performance than double glazing; low-e coatings reflect heat back into the house; cavities filled with argon or krypton reduce heat loss; an improved window U-value, a more comfortable indoor temperature and reduced condensation. A sketch should show the three panes, spacers and cavities. Solar panel: a solar collector absorbs solar radiation and converts it to heat, usually on a south-facing roof or secure ground-level fixing, working with other forms of heating and reducing CO2 emissions; types include flat-plate and evacuated-tube collectors, and tubes can be mounted to follow the sun. The scheme also lists photovoltaic panels: a coherent explanation of either is acceptable, but a photovoltaic panel produces electricity, not heat. Cordless drill: battery operated with rechargeable batteries, so not directly connected to AC mains power in use; features similar to a mains drill, including hammer action; used for driving screws, with a clutch to prevent damage to screw heads; right-angle versions for tight spaces; several power and speed settings, light low-voltage drills for DIY and heavier higher-voltage drills for robust work. A sketch should show the drill body, chuck and battery. Skirting board: a decorative board fitted at the junction of a wall and floor, giving a neat finish; hardwood, softwood or MDF in various lengths and profiles; typical sections from 100 mm × 15 mm to 200 mm × 20 mm; mitred at internal and external corners. A sketch should show the board fixed at the wall–floor junction. Compression fitting: a plumbing joint for copper or PVC pipes, made of brass or PVC in a range of sizes; the pipe ends are cut square, the nut and olive are fitted over the pipe, the pipe is pushed into the fitting and the nut is tightened to compress the olive into a watertight joint; PTFE tape may be used. A sketch should show the body, nut, olive and pipe. Natural seasoning: a traditional method of reducing the moisture content of timber; planks are stacked parallel with spaces between, separated by stickers (usually about 25 mm × 15 mm), in an open shed on a clean, dry, level base such as brick piers, and dried by the prevailing weather; plank ends are painted to prevent splitting; one species per stack; moisture content falls to about 18–22%, in equilibrium with the surrounding air; cheap because it uses no electrical energy, but slow and the rate cannot be controlled. A sketch should show the stacked planks, stickers and cover. Concrete lintel: a reinforced concrete beam spanning a door or window opening, carrying the blockwork or brickwork above and transferring the load to the wall at either side; cast in situ or, more commonly, pre-stressed; the length depends on the opening width and the imposed loads, and pre-stressed lintels come in a range of lengths and widths. A sketch should show the lintel bearing on the wall either side of the opening. Radon barrier: a flexible membrane placed under the floor and extended through the external walls to prevent radon gas entering the building; fitted over the whole floor area as one complete, unbroken layer with all joints taped and sealed, including around service pipes; usually laid over sand blinding (which protects it) and beneath the insulation; it replaces the damp proof membrane; installed with care by trained personnel so it is not damaged. Only a membrane rated and detailed as a radon barrier does this job.

stem: The sketch shows a railway keepers cottage built over 130 years ago. These traditional cottages can be seen at railway crossing points throughout our rural landscape. They form an important part of our built heritage.
questionText: A survey of the cottage reveals: 500 mm solid external wall of stone construction, uninsulated, with an internal lime render; uninsulated traditional cut roof with natural slate; single-glazed, softwood sliding sash windows. Select any two of the above areas and, using notes and freehand sketches, describe in detail the steps involved in upgrading the thermal performance of each area selected in a manner that respects the original character of the cottage.

rows.verbatim: Steps involved in upgrading the thermal performance of each area selected
rows.contextNote: Any two of the three areas, each notes 8 and sketches 12 = 20, respecting the cottage’s character. Stone wall: keep the wall breathable, with layers more vapour-permeable towards the outside and no impermeable vapour barriers; use hygroscopic natural insulation (hemp/hempcrete, lime, wood fibre, cork, sheep’s wool); rake out and repoint with lime mortar by hand (joints raked to twice their width, dampened first, filled in stages, protected with hessian while it carbonates); apply hempcrete internally and allow 4–6 weeks to dry, then lime render, or a three-coat lime plaster (scud coat, haired scratch coat, float coat, lime-putty finish). Cut roof: remove and set aside the slates, cleaning only their undersides; check and repair decayed rafters, wallplate and fascia in the same species and profile with traditional joints; treat new timber (boron); fit a vapour-permeable breathable membrane with counter-battens for ventilation; insulate with hygroscopic materials (sheep’s wool between rafters, wood fibre board above or below); keep the roof ventilated; re-lay the slates with the heaviest at the eaves, replacing broken ones with reclaimed slate; period cast-iron rainwater goods. Sash windows: repair rather than replace the original sashes, using a specialist conservation joiner; remove sashes and glass carefully, recording positions; replace only rotten timber in the same species and profiles with traditional joints and animal glue; free the pulleys, renew the sash cords and reuse the weights; reglaze with linseed-oil putty (salvaged or sourced float glass); repaint with non-toxic paint; add discreet secondary glazing to cut heat loss; record the repair.

options: Thermal upgrading of solid stone external wall
Thermal upgrading of traditional cut roof
Original sliding sash windows-softwood and single glazed

stem: The sketch shows a railway keepers cottage built over 130 years ago. These traditional cottages can be seen at railway crossing points throughout our rural landscape. They form an important part of our built heritage.
questionText: Discuss the importance of any two of the following when restoring traditional heritage buildings: conservation of original materials; breathable structure; respect for our built heritage.

rows.verbatim: Importance when restoring traditional heritage buildings
rows.contextNote: Any two of the three principles, each discussion/notes 10. Conservation of original materials: preserves authenticity and significance; traditional materials have qualities modern replacements cannot match; repair is usually more sustainable than replacement; original fabric records the building’s age and history. Breathable structure: moisture is not trapped in walls, floors and roofs; less risk of damp, mould and timber decay; protects masonry from freeze–thaw and salt damage; healthier indoor environment; the building performs as originally intended. Respect for our built heritage: understand the building’s significance before work; preserve distinctive features and craftsmanship; make sympathetic alterations; follow conservation principles and guidelines; heritage buildings are irreplaceable cultural resources.

stem: A continuous thermal envelope is essential to prevent thermal bridging in a dwelling. The drawing shows a vertical section through the external leaf of a bungalow having a 450 mm concrete block wall with a 250 mm full-fill insulated cavity. The house has a truss roof and an insulated concrete ground floor. The window frame is thermally broken.
questionText: Using notes and freehand sketches, show best practice design detailing that will prevent the formation of a thermal bridge at any three locations circled on the drawing.

rows.verbatim: Best practice design detailing to prevent thermal bridging
rows.contextNote: Any three of the four circled locations, each note 8 and sketches 8 = 16, showing the continuous insulation line. Wall and roof junction: wall and roof insulation meeting to keep the envelope continuous; a thermal break at the wallplate (insulated barrier or thermal blocks); cavity insulation continued and the eaves detailed to avoid a cold bridge; no direct structural or steel connections bridging the insulation. Window Head: wall insulation continuous with the window frame insulation; thermally broken frame and insulated cavity closers at the opening; insulated lintels or thermal-break details above the window; airtight seals around the frame. Window cill: wall insulation and cavity closers continued around the opening; an insulated cill detail or insulation behind the concrete cill; thermally broken frame with insulated perimeter seals; airtight frame-to-wall junction. Wall and floor junction: floor and wall insulation continuous; insulated slab-edge (perimeter) detail; cavity insulation taken down to meet the floor insulation; thermal blocks where the slab abuts the external wall, with no exposed concrete bridging inside to outside.

questionText:
(a) Discuss in detail the importance of any two of the following in maintaining a positive health and safety culture among workers on a construction site: safety training; health and safety officer; risk assessment audit.

(b) Outline one possible risk to personal safety associated with each of the following: working in a deep trench; installing insulation in an attic space; repairing a chimney capping.

(c) For each risk discussed at 2(b) above, show, using notes and freehand sketches, two best practice guidelines that should be observed to reduce the possibility of injury to a worker undertaking each task.

rows.verbatim: The importance of any two in maintaining a positive health and safety culture
rows.contextNote: Any two of the three, 6 each, discussing why each matters to a positive health and safety culture. Safety training: Safe Pass is mandatory and kept current through refresher courses; training builds awareness of site risks and the skills to identify them and follow best practice; specialist tickets for machinery and vehicles; monitoring and enforcing safe work practices; it may be a condition of the insurance provider. Health and safety officer: provides induction and ongoing training (working at heights, machinery use); develops emergency response plans; keeps first aid and emergency equipment available; ensures the correct PPE is worn; carries out safety inspections and risk assessments; reviews the safety statement; investigates, records and reports accidents. Risk assessment audit: provides a safe working environment; evaluates compliance with safety regulations and policies; identifies hazards and puts control measures in place where a risk cannot be eliminated (for fire: alarms, evacuation signage, drills, extinguishers); recommends improvements; identifies training needs; reduces accidents and liability.

One risk outlined. Such as: workers seriously injured or buried if the trench sides collapse; machinery or vehicles falling in; materials stored too close to the edge causing a collapse; falling into an unguarded trench; materials falling in; nearby structures undermined.

rows.verbatim: Installing insulation in an attic space
rows.contextNote: One risk outlined. Such as: falling through the plasterboard ceiling; injury when cutting the insulation; skin or eye irritation without a coverall, gloves and goggles; electrocution from exposed wires; fire if insulation covers recessed lights; lung damage from inhaled machine-made mineral fibres (MMMFs).

One risk outlined. Such as: falling or slipping from the roof or from a ladder; equipment or materials dropped on people below; scaffolding collapsing; falling from lifting machinery such as a cherry picker.
Note 3 and sketch 3. Such as: a trench box or shuttering to support the sides; battering back (sloping) the sides; a barrier with a toe board, or a temporary cover over a vacant trench.

A second, different guideline: note 3 and sketch 3. Such as: no materials, machinery or vehicles near the edge; a clearly marked exclusion zone and signage; PPE (hard hat, eye protection, footwear); digging in suitable, not wet, conditions; an engineer’s survey of nearby structures.

Note 3 and sketch 3. Such as: crawl boards to spread the load across the joists, or walking only on the joists and never on the plasterboard ceiling; a hooded coverall and gloves; an appropriate dust mask.
A second, different guideline: note 3 and sketch 3. Such as: safety goggles; non-combustible protection covers over downlighters; cutting insulation in a well-ventilated area; kneepads.
Note 3 and sketch 3. Such as: a safety harness or other fall protection; scaffolding around the stack erected by certified personnel, tied to the house or chimney, with safety rails and toe boards.

A second, different guideline: note 3 and sketch 3. Such as: toe boards and netting against falling objects; ladders secured and extending 1 metre past the scaffolding platform; a cherry picker operated by certified personnel on a level surface, with workers securely attached.

stem: An airtight external building envelope is important in the design of a dwelling house.
questionText: The drawing shows an outline section of a two-storey house having a 450 mm external concrete block wall with a 250 mm full-fill insulated cavity. The house has a truss roof and a first floor of timber construction. The external door has a thermally broken frame. A Mechanical Ventilation with Heat Recovery system supplies ventilation through ceiling ducts. Using notes and freehand sketches, show best practice design detailing that will prevent air leakage at any three of the locations circled on the drawing.

rows.verbatim: Best practice design detailing to prevent air leakage at any three of the locations circled
rows.contextNote: Any three of the four circled locations, each notes 8 and sketches 8 = 16, showing the continuous airtight layer. Head of external door: seal the thermally broken door frame to the reveal of the inner block wall with plasterable airtightness tape, then plaster over the tape; or airtightness paint on the reveal before plastering, or slabbing and skimming. First floor junction with external wall: make the wall airtight where the joists bear — an airtightness membrane sealed with airtight silicone or plasterable tape, or sand cement render or airtightness paint; tape each joist where it breaks the airtightness barrier; seal the floor/wall and roof/wall junctions with tape or paint. Wallplate level: an airtightness membrane under the ceiling joists, wrapped onto the wallplate and down onto the first block below it, fixed to the wall with plasterable airtightness tape or a bead of airtight silicone, then scrim or mesh and sand cement plaster. MVHR duct protruding through the ceiling: an airtightness membrane under the joists, sealed to the duct with a self-adhesive grommet fixed to the membrane, or by carefully taping the duct to the membrane with airtightness tape.

stem: The sketch shows the proposed design of a Passive House which is to be constructed in a rural setting.
questionText:
(a) Using notes and freehand sketches, discuss the importance of any two of the following in Passive House design: building form; foundation design; space heating energy demand.

(b) Using notes and freehand sketches, suggest a preferred orientation for the house shown. Show the sun path on your sketch. Discuss two benefits to the homeowner of your preferred orientation.

(c) Solar overheating may occur during the summer months in the house shown. Using notes and freehand sketches, suggest two ways to reduce the possibility of solar overheating while respecting the character of this house design.

rows.verbatim: Discuss the importance of any two in Passive House design
rows.contextNote: Any two of the three, each notes 5 and sketches 5 = 10. Building form: a compact, simple rectangular form with the smallest surface area (A/V ratio 0.7 or less) to cut heat loss, materials and cost; a narrow plan, one room deep, to maximise solar gain; clean lines in walls and roof that make airtightness easy. Foundation design: insulated ring-beam or passive raft foundations wrapped in insulation to eliminate thermal bridging; thermal blocks in the inner-leaf rising wall; 50–100 mm edge insulation at the floor/wall junction; thermally broken wall ties; a U-value of 0.10–0.15 W/m²K. Space heating energy demand: passive house space-heating demand of no more than 15 kWh/m² per year; quality workmanship in airtightness and insulation; eliminating thermal bridges; solar gain through well-designed fenestration; solar shading, thermal mass and controlled ventilation to keep about 20 °C all year.
Freehand sketch of the house showing the preferred orientation and the sun path.
Such as: the long axis with the largest amount of glazing facing south to maximise solar gain, with minimal glazing on the north.
The sun path shown on the sketch relative to north and the house.
Point 3 and discussion 3. Such as: lower energy bills, as solar gains reduce the need for artificial lighting and heating.
A second, different benefit: point 3 and discussion 3. Such as: lower carbon dioxide emissions from less artificial heating; a bright, airy home that enhances wellbeing.

Notes 3 and sketches 3. Such as: dynamic (electrochromic) glass that tints in response to light, heat or an electrical signal; or mature deciduous trees that block the summer sun and let winter sun through.

A second, different method: notes 3 and sketches 3. Such as: a brise soleil on the south side; internal or external shutters closed against the midday summer sun; high thermal mass (polished concrete floor, exposed stone walls) to even out temperatures.

(b) Select one of the above options and, using notes and freehand sketches, show a proposed external design and internal layout for an attractive study/family space. Show in your design how the proposed space is to link with the surrounding rear garden.

(c) Discuss two advantages of designing a space that links with the rear garden.

rows.contextNote: An advantage of the single-storey extension at A, discussed for this house (3). Such as: saves on construction and insulation costs; conserves space in the rear garden; more efficient energy use, as it minimises the area of external walling; more freedom in using and dividing the total living space.

A second, different advantage of the extension at A (3). Such as: easy, economical connection to existing services (space heating, plumbing, ventilation, electrical distribution); a compact plan that supports regular social interaction across the generations of the family.

A disadvantage of the extension at A (3). Such as: disturbs the well-proportioned original layout; creates a large undifferentiated space that needs careful design; can reduce the natural lighting and ventilation of the kitchen/dining room; more energy for lighting and heating a large space.

A second, different disadvantage of the extension at A (3). Such as: fewer discrete rooms for a quieter environment; may spoil the view from the existing kitchen and dining area; continuity of insulation and weatherproofing at the roof and wall abutment; spanning the larger opening in the existing external wall may need strengthening and RSJs; misses the chance to connect the garden with the living spaces.

Such as: keeps the existing relationship between the kitchen/dining area and the outside; minimises disruption during construction; maintains natural lighting to the existing rooms; greater privacy in a distinct room in the garden.

questionText: Discuss the importance of any two of the following in the eco-refurbishment of an old house built in the vernacular tradition: respect for local character; breathable structure; reuse of materials.

rows.contextNote: Any two of the three, 10 each, as a developed discussion; the scheme does not split the 10 into points. Respect for local character: vernacular houses evolved from their location, built simply and modestly from local materials and labour, so refurbishment keeps materials, methods and detailing simple, retains the historic character and the unity of the row of cottages, upgrades the fabric first, and takes advice from a conservation officer, architect, engineer or designer. Breathable structure: moisture moves gradually from the inside through the walls and roof and is not trapped, preventing surface and interstitial condensation; natural, hygroscopic insulation and finishes (lime, hemp, cork, wood fibreboard, sheep’s wool, lime renders and plasters) let it move; vapour barriers and vapour-resistant materials are not usually appropriate in older buildings, and layers should become more permeable from inside to outside. Reuse of materials: examine the whole house to see what can be reused; replace only the decayed portions of roof members (splice rafter ends, wall plate in the same timber); replace decayed fascia and soffit to the identical profile; lift, number and store floorboards and skirtings for reuse, replacing damaged boards with similar salvaged ones to keep the patina of age.

questionText: A row of single-storey cottages is shown in the sketch. One of the cottages is in need of significant refurbishment. A survey of the cottage reveals: un-insulated traditional cut roof with natural slates; softwood windows, single-glazed with sliding sash; un-insulated suspended timber floor. Select any two of the areas at 4(b) above and, using notes and freehand sketches, describe the steps involved in upgrading each area selected in a manner that respects the appearance and character of the original cottages.

rows.verbatim: Two areas for upgrading - roof, windows, floor
rows.contextNote: Any two of the three surveyed areas, each notes 10 and sketches 10 = 20, describing the upgrading steps in a way that respects the appearance and character of the original cottages. Roof: retain as much historic fabric as possible; remove, number and store the slates and reuse them (slates from the rear placed on the front for uniformity); inspect the members and replace only decayed portions; replace impermeable sarking felt with a vapour-diffuse membrane; insulate with hygroscopic materials (sheep’s wool between the rafters, wood fibreboard above and below) with counter battens for ventilation, or, as the scheme’s other option, insulation with a ventilation path and a continuous taped vapour barrier on the warm side behind an insulated service cavity. Sliding sash windows: maintain and repair before replacing; survey, number and remove the sashes; repair damaged wood with a similar species, sand, seal and repaint; remove cracked putty and re-glaze with linseed oil putty; check the pulleys and cords; then keep the existing glass, or fit draught-proof seals and double-glazed units where the rebates are deep enough, or fit secondary glazing inside. Suspended timber floor: determine the floor’s historical significance; record and number the floorboards and skirting, remove and store them; check the sub-floor ventilation; replace decayed joists or boards; fit insulation between the joists on netting or battens, friction tight with no gaps; fit a breather membrane and replace the floorboards as labelled.

stem: The elevation and ground floor plan of a house are shown. The house has three bedrooms and a bathroom upstairs. The external walls are of timber frame construction with a rendered concrete block outer leaf. The house is designed to maximise solar energy, as shown, and to have low environmental impact.
questionText: Using notes and freehand sketches, discuss the importance of any two of the following in designing a house to have low environmental impact: compact form; flexible design; low maintenance.

rows.contextNote: Any two of the three, each notes 5 and sketches 5 = 10. Compact form: a reduced external surface area minimises heat loss and the materials needed to enclose the living space; less concrete and so lower carbon emissions; a smaller heated air volume; a house one room wide is easier to heat by passive solar gain; less land used and less visual impact. Flexible design: the dwelling can respond over time to changes in lifestyle and needs without major structural change, extending its useful life; a bathroom designed for lifetime use; a home office or occasional bedroom easily made; a wall to the hallway removable to form a larger open-plan area; easier retrofitting of new technologies. Low maintenance: reduces the energy and materials used over the dwelling’s lifetime and delays its replacement; keeps the energy-saving features at peak efficiency for longer; robust construction; keeps the attractive, unobtrusive appearance for longer.

stem: It is proposed to design the external envelope of a dwelling house to be thermal bridge free. The drawing shows an outline section through a two-storey house having a 450 mm external concrete block wall with a 250 mm full-fill insulated cavity. The roof is a traditional cut roof, the first floor has tongue-and-groove flooring on timber joists and the ground floor is an insulated solid concrete floor.
questionText: Select any three locations from those circled on the drawing and, using notes and freehand sketches, show best practice design detailing that will prevent the formation of a thermal bridge at each location selected.

rows.contextNote: Any three of the four circled locations, each notes 8 and sketches 8 = 16, showing the insulation kept continuous so that no thermal bridge forms. Junction of roof and wall at eaves: 60 mm rigid insulation board; 400 mm fibreglass insulation; a 60 mm cavity closer; an autoclaved aerated concrete (AAC) block; 250 mm full-fill cavity insulation. Junction of upper floors and external walls: joists hung on the inside leaf, on metal hangers or resin-anchored bolts, with no penetration of the leaf and cavity; the wall plastered for airtightness. Window cill: insulation at the back of the cill so it does not bridge the cavity; a high-density proprietary cavity closer; 250 mm full-fill cavity insulation; airtightness tape to the triple-glazed window frame. Ground floors abutting external walls: cavity insulation carried down at least 225 mm below the top of the finished floor; an 80 mm perimeter insulation strip between the slab and the inner leaf; 150–300 mm insulation under the slab; 100 mm AAC blocks below ground level.

options: Junction of roof and wall at eaves
Junction of upper floors and external walls

questionText: Using notes and freehand sketches, discuss in detail the importance of any two of the following in the design of a Passive House: airtight building envelope; space heating demand; indoor air quality.

rows.verbatim: Design of a Passive House - any 2
rows.contextNote: Any two of the three, each notes 8 and sketches 8 = 16. Airtight building envelope: build tight and ventilate right; an unbroken air barrier on the warm side of the insulation, taped at every junction (wall/floor, wall/window, wall/door, ceiling/wall, chimney/ceiling), prevents unregulated air leakage and heat loss and lets the fresh-air intake be controlled; a service cavity keeps services from puncturing it; grommets seal pipes and cables; a blower door test checks it. Space heating demand: the energy needed to keep 20 °C indoors all year, not including hot water; a Passive House limits it to 15 kWh/m² per year or less, with a heating load of no more than 10 W/m²; the 2015 scheme also cites a primary energy demand of no more than 120 kWh/m² per year. Indoor air quality: greater airtightness needs a designed ventilation system that supplies clean, warm, filtered fresh air; mechanical ventilation with heat recovery extracts moist air from the kitchen, utility and bathrooms and passes it through a heat exchanger without mixing it with the incoming air; filters changed every three to six months; relative humidity of 30% to 60%; 0.3 to 0.6 air changes per hour.

stem: The sketch shows a proposed external wall design for a new house. The external wall is constructed using Insulated Concrete Formwork (ICF).
questionText:
Calculate the U-value of the wall, given the construction has the following sequence and data: Acrylic external render thickness 12 mm; external insulation thickness 150 mm; concrete thickness 150 mm; internal insulation thickness 50 mm; internal plasterboard thickness 12.5 mm; internal skim coat thickness 4 mm.
Thermal data of the external wall: resistance of external surface (R) 0.048 m² °C/W; conductivity of acrylic external render (k) 0.670 W/m °C; conductivity of external insulation (k) 0.030 W/m °C; conductivity of concrete (k) 1.280 W/m °C; conductivity of internal insulation (k) 0.030 W/m °C; conductivity of plasterboard (k) 0.250 W/m °C; resistivity of skim coat (r) 5.550 m °C/W; resistance of internal surface (R) 0.122 m² °C/W.

rows.contextNote: A clear table of the materials with their conductivity or resistivity, thickness in metres and resistance.

Eight resistances, 3 each, by R = T/k (or R = T × r for the skim coat): external surface 0.048 (given); acrylic render 0.012/0.670 = 0.018; external insulation 0.150/0.030 = 5.000; concrete 0.150/1.280 = 0.117; internal insulation 0.050/0.030 = 1.667; plasterboard 0.0125/0.250 = 0.050; skim coat 0.004 × 5.550 = 0.022; internal surface 0.122 (given). All in m²°C/W.
Total resistance Rt = 7.044 m²°C/W (the sum of all the resistances).
U = 1 ÷ Rt = 1 ÷ 7.044 = 0.142 W/m²°C, with units.

stem: The sketch shows a bungalow which has been retrofitted. The owners have engaged skilled labour in the upgrade of their bungalow to meet the EnerPHit Passive House design standard.
questionText:
(a) Using notes and freehand sketches, discuss the importance of any two of the following when carrying out a retrofit to achieve the EnerPHit Passive House design standard: airtightness; windows; building fabric.

(b) Using notes and freehand sketches, discuss in detail how each of the following could be improved, when upgrading an existing building to meet the EnerPHit standard: indoor air quality; space heating.

(c) Discuss two advantages of using qualified skilled labour when retrofitting a house to meet EnerPHit Passive House standards.

rows.verbatim: Discuss the importance of any two in EnerPHit design standard
rows.contextNote: Any two of the three, each notes 6 and sketches 6 = 12. EnerPHit is reached through the five Passive House principles (insulation, limited thermal bridging, triple glazing, airtightness, MVHR), modelled in the PHPP design tool; its space heating demand limit is 25 kWh/m² per year (Passive House 15). Airtightness: Air leakage prevented with airtightness membranes, airtight boards and tapes in timber frame and roofs, and a sand-cement scratch coat, plaster and airtightness paint in block walls; checks for leakage at each stage and a full airtightness test at the end; the EnerPHit target is under 1.0 air changes per hour at 50 Pascals (Passive House 0.6); without airtightness the insulation cannot perform. Windows: Passive House triple-glazed windows of 0.80 W/m²K or less (EnerPHit, installed, 0.85 W/m²K or less); frames in line with the external insulation to avoid a thermal bridge; shading and ventilation planned against summer overheating. Building fabric: Insulation increased to roof, floor and walls (U-value 0.120 W/m²K or less for EnerPHit) by cavity, external or internal insulation; quality workmanship to avoid thermal bridges; external insulation continued below ground level; airtightness and insulation achieved together.

Such as: mechanical ventilation with heat recovery (MVHR) supplying fresh air and recovering heat, with regular filter changes; low-VOC materials, finishes and furnishings; humidity kept at 30–50% with humidity-controlled ventilation; air-quality sensors; openable windows in every room.
Freehand sketches of the improvement, such as the MVHR supply and extract routes.

Such as: continuous high-quality insulation without thermal bridges; high-performance glazing and doors with sealed junctions; an air-source or ground-source heat pump (coefficient of performance about 5:1) with underfloor heating; MVHR heat recovery; passive solar gain and thermal mass, with shading against overheating, for a steady 20 °C.
Freehand sketches of the improvement.
Point 2 and discussion 4. Such as: expertise in the complex EnerPHit requirements and best practice; quality workmanship so every component is installed correctly and the energy targets are met.

A second, different advantage: point 2 and discussion 4. Such as: efficient, on-time completion; compliance with regulations, including airtightness; problem solving on site; long-term performance, so the disruptive retrofit need not be repeated.

stem: “Buildings have an impact on the environment at every stage of their lifecycle. Materials have to be quarried, mined or harvested, transported to factories and manufactured. The final products have to be transported to site, lifted into place and fixed in position. The buildings have to be operated, heated and cooled. Over a 60 year life cycle, components fail, roof finishes fail and need replacement, finishes spoil and need repainting and replacement. Eventually the building ceases to provide its function and needs to be deconstructed and all its components disposed by landfill, incineration, recycling or direct reuse.” Adapted from: Towards a circular economy in construction. Published by: Irish Green Building Council.
questionText: Discuss the above statement in detail.

rows.verbatim: Discussion Point 1 (4 for point, 6 for discussion)
rows.contextNote: Point 4 and discussion 6. Such as: the environmental impact of a dwelling at every stage of its lifecycle; weighing the embodied energy of materials against their operational energy — short-lived components carry a higher carbon footprint.

rows.verbatim: Discussion Point 2 (4 for point, 6 for discussion)
rows.contextNote: Point 4 and discussion 6. Such as: Environmental Product Declarations (EPD), “cradle to grave”, measuring global warming potential and other impacts, with the Irish EPD programme of the Irish Green Building Council.

rows.verbatim: Discussion Point 3 (4 for point, 6 for discussion)
rows.contextNote: Point 4 and discussion 6. Such as: the circular economy — materials kept in loops of reuse, remanufacture and recycling at their highest value, the opposite of take-make-dispose; careful design that needs less heating and cooling over the building’s life. Three distinct, well-argued points are needed.

stem: An extension to a house has a highly insulated flat roof with a waterproof roof covering, as shown.
questionText:
Calculate the U-value of the roof, given the construction has the following sequence and data: Waterproof covering thickness 2 mm; roof insulation thickness 150 mm; plywood decking thickness 20 mm; clear cavity between roof joists thickness 200 mm; ceiling insulation thickness 50 mm; plasterboard thickness 12.5 mm.
Thermal data of the flat roof: resistance of external surface (R) 0.048 m² °C/W; resistivity of waterproof covering (r) 6.250 m °C/W; conductivity of roof insulation (k) 0.022 W/m °C; conductivity of plywood (k) 0.130 W/m °C; resistance of clear cavity (R) 0.170 m² °C/W; conductivity of ceiling insulation (k) 0.022 W/m °C; conductivity of plasterboard (k) 0.250 W/m °C; resistance of internal surface (R) 0.122 m² °C/W.

rows.contextNote: Eight resistances, 3 each, by R = T/k (or R = T × r): external surface 0.048 (given); waterproof covering 0.002 × 6.250 = 0.013; roof insulation 0.150/0.022 = 6.818; plywood 0.020/0.130 = 0.154; clear cavity 0.170 (given); ceiling insulation 0.050/0.022 = 2.273; plasterboard 0.0125/0.250 = 0.050; internal surface 0.122 (given). All in m²°C/W.
Total resistance Rt = 9.647 m²°C/W (the sum of all the resistances).
U = 1 ÷ Rt = 1 ÷ 9.647 = 0.104 W/m²°C, with units.

stem: An extension to a house has a highly insulated flat roof with a waterproof roof covering, as shown.
questionText:
(a) Calculate the U-value of the roof, given the construction has the following sequence and data: Waterproof covering thickness 2 mm; roof insulation thickness 150 mm; plywood decking thickness 20 mm; clear cavity between roof joists thickness 200 mm; ceiling insulation thickness 50 mm; plasterboard thickness 12.5 mm.
Thermal data of the flat roof: resistance of external surface (R) 0.048 m² °C/W; resistivity of waterproof covering (r) 6.250 m °C/W; conductivity of roof insulation (k) 0.022 W/m °C; conductivity of plywood (k) 0.130 W/m °C; resistance of clear cavity (R) 0.170 m² °C/W; conductivity of ceiling insulation (k) 0.022 W/m °C; conductivity of plasterboard (k) 0.250 W/m °C; resistance of internal surface (R) 0.122 m² °C/W.

(b) Using the U-value of the roof obtained at 5(a) above and the following data, calculate the cost of heat lost annually through this roof: dimensions of flat roof 8.5 metres × 4.5 metres; average internal temperature 18 °C; average external temperature 5 °C; heating period 8 hours daily for 36 weeks per annum; cost of oil €1.25 per litre; calorific value of oil 37350 kJ per litre; 1000 watts: 1 kJ per second.

(c) Using notes and a freehand sketch, show best practice design detailing that will prevent the formation of a thermal bridge at the abutment of the flat roof and external concrete block wall with a full-fill insulated cavity.

rows.contextNote: Eight resistances, 3 each, by R = T/k (or R = T × r): external surface 0.048 (given); waterproof covering 0.002 × 6.250 = 0.013; roof insulation 0.150/0.022 = 6.818; plywood 0.020/0.130 = 0.154; clear cavity 0.170 (given); ceiling insulation 0.050/0.022 = 2.273; plasterboard 0.0125/0.250 = 0.050; internal surface 0.122 (given). All in m²°C/W.
Total resistance Rt = 9.647 m²°C/W (the sum of all the resistances).
U = 1 ÷ Rt = 1 ÷ 9.647 = 0.104 W/m²°C, with units.
Heat loss = U-value × area × temperature difference = 0.104 × 38.25 × (18 − 5) = 51.714 watts (joules per second).

rows.verbatim: Heating duration - calculation for one year
rows.contextNote: Heating period = 60 × 60 × 7 × 8 × 36 = 7,257,600 seconds (2,016 hours).

rows.verbatim: Litres of oil - calculation for one year

rows.verbatim: Discuss two Passive House design features
rows.contextNote: Any two of the three, each notes 5 and sketches 5 = 10. Thermally efficient building envelope: an unbroken line of insulation and airtightness around the whole building, with every element at its optimum performance; a constant, predictable internal temperature; lower energy use, costs and carbon.

stem: “People regardless of age, size, ability or disability are positively contributing to the social, economic and cultural life of our communities. However, finding suitable and appropriate homes that can accommodate our changing needs over time can be difficult - whether for families with young children, a person with a temporary or permanent injury, someone with a disability, or an older person living independently. stem: The proposed external wall design detail for a new house is a 215 mm single leaf wall of solid block construction with external insulation, as shown.
questionText:
Calculate the U-value of the wall, given the construction has the following sequence and data: Acrylic external render thickness 8 mm; external insulation thickness 150 mm; external scratch coat thickness 10 mm; concrete block thickness 215 mm; internal plaster thickness 12 mm.
Thermal data of the external wall: resistance of external surface (R) 0.048 m2 ⁰C/W; conductivity of acrylic external render (k) 0.670 W/m ⁰C; conductivity of external insulation (k) 0.031 W/m ⁰C; conductivity of external scratch coat (k) 2.170 W/m ⁰C; conductivity of concrete blockwork (k) 1.440 W/m ⁰C; resistivity of internal plaster (r) 4.550 m ⁰C/W; resistance of internal surface (R) 0.122 m2 ⁰C/W.

rows.contextNote: A clear table of the materials with their conductivity or resistivity, thickness in metres and resistance.

Seven resistances, 3 each, by R = T/k (or R = T × r for the plaster): external surface 0.048 (given); acrylic render 0.008/0.670 = 0.012; external insulation 0.150/0.031 = 4.839; scratch coat 0.010/2.170 = 0.005; blockwork 0.215/1.44 = 0.149; internal plaster 0.012 × 4.550 = 0.055; internal surface 0.122 (given). All in m²°C/W.
Total resistance Rt = 5.229 m²°C/W (the sum of all the resistances).
U = 1 ÷ Rt = 1 ÷ 5.229 = 0.191 W/m²°C, with units.

stem: The proposed external wall design detail for a new house is a 215 mm single leaf wall of solid block construction with external insulation, as shown.
questionText:
(a) Calculate the U-value of the wall, given the construction has the following sequence and data: Acrylic external render thickness 8 mm; external insulation thickness 150 mm; external scratch coat thickness 10 mm; concrete block thickness 215 mm; internal plaster thickness 12 mm.
Thermal data of the external wall: resistance of external surface (R) 0.048 m2 ⁰C/W; conductivity of acrylic external render (k) 0.670 W/m ⁰C; conductivity of external insulation (k) 0.031 W/m ⁰C; conductivity of external scratch coat (k) 2.170 W/m ⁰C; conductivity of concrete blockwork (k) 1.440 W/m ⁰C; resistivity of internal plaster (r) 4.550 m ⁰C/W; resistance of internal surface (R) 0.122 m2 ⁰C/W.

(b) Using the U-value of the wall obtained at 5(a) above and the following data, calculate the cost of heat lost annually through this wall: area of external wall 144 m2; average internal temperature 20 ⁰C; average external temperature 5 ⁰C; heating period 10 hours daily for 37 weeks per annum; cost of oil 97 cent per litre; calorific value of oil 37350 kJ per litre; 1000 watts: 1 kJ per second.

(c) It is proposed to redesign the above external wall and upgrade its thermal properties to meet the Passive House standard by increasing the width of external insulation in the design. Calculate the thickness of additional external insulation required to achieve a U-value of 0.12 W/m2 ⁰C.

rows.contextNote: A clear table of the materials with their conductivity or resistivity, thickness in metres and resistance.

Seven resistances, 3 each, by R = T/k (or R = T × r for the plaster): external surface 0.048 (given); acrylic render 0.008/0.670 = 0.012; external insulation 0.150/0.031 = 4.839; scratch coat 0.010/2.170 = 0.005; blockwork 0.215/1.44 = 0.149; internal plaster 0.012 × 4.550 = 0.055; internal surface 0.122 (given). All in m²°C/W.
Total resistance Rt = 5.229 m²°C/W (the sum of all the resistances).
U = 1 ÷ Rt = 1 ÷ 5.229 = 0.191 W/m²°C, with units.
Heat loss = U-value × area × temperature difference = 0.191 × 144 × (20 − 5) = 413.068 watts (joules per second).
Heating period = 60 × 60 × 7 × 10 × 37 = 9,324,000 seconds (2,590 hours).

rows.verbatim: Litres of oil for one year

rows.contextNote: Annual cost = 103.118 × €0.97 = €100.02. The scheme’s alternative one-line method gives the same €100.02.

rows.verbatim: Resistance for U- value for 0.12 W/m2 °c (using R=1/U)
rows.contextNote: Required resistance = 1 ÷ 0.12 = 8.333 m²°C/W.

rows.verbatim: Resistance from calculated U-value from part (a)
rows.contextNote: Resistance of the wall from (a) = 1 ÷ 0.191 = 5.229 m²°C/W.
Difference = 8.333 − 5.229 = 3.104 m²°C/W.

rows.verbatim: Required thickness of insulation in mm.
rows.contextNote: Additional insulation = 96 mm (95 or 97 mm accepted). Alternative calculation methods are acceptable.

stem: The sketch shows a proposed external wall design detail for a new house of timber frame construction.
questionText:
Calculate the U-value of the wall, given the construction has the following sequence and data: External brick thickness 100 mm; clear cavity width 50 mm; orientated strand board (OSB) thickness 9 mm; timber stud thickness 175 mm; cellulose insulation between studs thickness 175 mm; orientated strand board (OSB) thickness 9 mm; plasterboard thickness 12.5 mm.
Thermal data of the external wall: resistance of external surface (R) 0.048 m2 ⁰C/W; resistivity of external brick (r) 1.300 m ⁰C/W; resistance of clear cavity (R) 0.440 m2 ⁰C/W; conductivity of OSB (k) 0.130 W/m ⁰C; conductivity of cellulose insulation (k) 0.039 W/m ⁰C; conductivity of OSB (k) 0.130 W/m ⁰C; conductivity of plasterboard (k) 0.250 W/m ⁰C; resistance of internal surface (R) 0.130 m2 ⁰C/W. Note: The timber studs need not be considered in your calculations.

rows.contextNote: Eight resistances, 3 each, by R = T/k (or R = T × r for the brick): external surface 0.048 (given); brick 0.1 × 1.300 = 0.130; cavity 0.440 (given); OSB 0.009/0.130 = 0.069; cellulose 0.175/0.039 = 4.487; OSB 0.069; plasterboard 0.0125/0.25 = 0.050; internal surface 0.130 (given). All in m²°C/W.
Total resistance Rt = 5.424 m²°C/W.
U = 1 ÷ Rt = 1 ÷ 5.424 = 0.184 W/m²°C, with units.

stem: A house built to nZEB standards has a highly insulated solid concrete ground floor with a hardwood finish, as shown.
questionText:
(a) Calculate the U-value of the floor, given the construction has the following sequence and data: Hardwood flooring thickness 20 mm; sand/cement fine screed thickness 65 mm; floor insulation thickness 200mm; concrete floor slab thickness 150 mm; radon barrier thickness 0.25 mm; sand blinding thickness 40 mm; hardcore thickness 200 mm; subsoil thickness 300 mm.
Thermal data of the ground floor: resistance of internal top surface of floor (R) 0.104 m2 ⁰C/W; conductivity of hardwood flooring (k) 6.666 W/m ⁰C; resistivity of fine screed (r) 1.410 m ⁰C/W; conductivity of floor insulation (k) 0.022 W/m ⁰C; conductivity of concrete floor slab (k) 1.280 W/m ⁰C; conductivity of radon barrier (k) 0.250 W/m ⁰C; conductivity of sand blinding (k) 0.160 W/m ⁰C; conductivity of hardcore (k) 1.350 W/m ⁰C; conductivity of subsoil (k) 1.600 W/m ⁰C.

(b) Using the U-value of the floor obtained at 5(a) above and the following data, calculate the cost of heat lost annually through this floor: dimensions of floor slab 6.5 metres × 9.0 metres; average internal temperature 20 ⁰C; average temperature of subsoil 6 ⁰C; heating period 9 hours daily for 39 weeks per annum; cost of oil 96 cent per litre; calorific value of oil 37350 kJ per litre; 1000 Watts: 1 kJ per second.

(c) Using notes and a freehand sketch, show best practice design detailing that will prevent the formation of a thermal bridge at the junction of the concrete floor and an external concrete block wall with a full-fill insulated cavity.

rows.contextNote: Nine resistances, 3 each, by R = T/k (or R = T × r for the screed): internal surface 0.104 (given); hardwood 0.02/6.666 = 0.003; screed 0.065 × 1.410 = 0.092; insulation 0.2/0.022 = 9.091; slab 0.15/1.28 = 0.117; radon barrier 0.00025/0.25 = 0.001; sand blinding 0.04/0.16 = 0.25; hardcore 0.2/1.35 = 0.148; subsoil 0.3/1.6 = 0.188. All in m²°C/W.
Total resistance Rt = 9.993 m²°C/W.
U = 1 ÷ Rt = 1 ÷ 9.993 = 0.10 W/m²°C, with units.
Heat loss = U-value × area × temperature difference = 0.10 × 58.5 × (20 − 6) = 81.9 watts (joules per second).
Heating period = 60 × 60 × 9 × 7 × 39 = 8,845,200 seconds (2,457 hours).

rows.verbatim: Litres of oil for one year

rows.contextNote: Annual cost = 19.39 × €0.96 = €18.62. The scheme’s alternative one-line method gives the same €18.62.

stem: The sketch shows a row of terraced townhouses built over 100 years ago. A young couple have purchased one of the houses and have decided to refurbish it as their family home.
questionText: The owners commissioned a survey of the house which revealed the following: traditional cut roof with natural slates; softwood sliding sash windows with single-glazing; solid external walls of brick construction, uninsulated and with internal lime render. Select any two of the above areas and, using notes and freehand sketches, describe in detail the steps involved in upgrading each area selected in a manner that respects the appearance and character of the original townhouses.

rows.contextNote: Any two of the three printed areas, each notes 10 and sketches 8 = 18. Traditional cut roof with natural slates: remove the slates carefully, clean only their undersides of lime parging, weigh and grade them and refit the heaviest at the eaves; replace decayed rafter ends, wallplate and fascia in the same species and profiles; a vapour-diffuse breathable membrane with counter battens; cast-iron rainwater goods; hygroscopic insulation such as sheep’s wool with woodfibre board, and a thoroughly ventilated roof. Softwood sliding sash windows with single - glazing: repair rather than replace, by a specialist conservation joiner; remove the sashes and glass carefully and record their positions; replace rotten timber in the same species with traditional joints and animal glue; free the pulleys, renew the cords and reuse the counter-balance weights; non-toxic paint; discreet secondary glazing. Solid external walls of brick construction, uninsulated and with internal lime render: never cement mortar; have the lime mortar analysed and matched (NHL strength, sand); rake out by hand to twice the joint width and repoint in stages, protected with hessian; internally, hempcrete or an insulating lime plaster system with a three-coat lime render.

stem: The sketch shows a row of terraced townhouses built over 100 years ago. A young couple have purchased one of the houses and have decided to refurbish it as their family home.
questionText:
(a) Discuss three benefits to the local community of refurbishing one of the townhouses as a family home.

(b) The owners commissioned a survey of the house which revealed the following: traditional cut roof with natural slates; softwood sliding sash windows with single-glazing; solid external walls of brick construction, uninsulated and with internal lime render. Select any two of the above areas and, using notes and freehand sketches, describe in detail the steps involved in upgrading each area selected in a manner that respects the appearance and character of the original townhouses.

rows.contextNote: Point 4 and discussion 4. Such as: sustaining the local social community — schools, parks and playgrounds; supporting local shops and cafés.
A second, different benefit. Such as: improving the physical fabric of the neighbourhood; easing the urban housing shortage.
A third, different benefit. Such as: pride that encourages neighbours to upgrade; keeping the residential architectural heritage; regeneration of the area.

Any two of the three printed areas, each notes 10 and sketches 8 = 18. Traditional cut roof with natural slates: remove the slates carefully, clean only their undersides of lime parging, weigh and grade them and refit the heaviest at the eaves; replace decayed rafter ends, wallplate and fascia in the same species and profiles; a vapour-diffuse breathable membrane with counter battens; cast-iron rainwater goods; hygroscopic insulation such as sheep’s wool with woodfibre board, and a thoroughly ventilated roof. Softwood sliding sash windows with single - glazing: repair rather than replace, by a specialist conservation joiner; remove the sashes and glass carefully and record their positions; replace rotten timber in the same species with traditional joints and animal glue; free the pulleys, renew the cords and reuse the counter-balance weights; non-toxic paint; discreet secondary glazing. Solid external walls of brick construction, uninsulated and with internal lime render: never cement mortar; have the lime mortar analysed and matched (NHL strength, sand); rake out by hand to twice the joint width and repoint in stages, protected with hessian; internally, hempcrete or an insulating lime plaster system with a three-coat lime render.

stem: The external wall of a house built in the 1990s is of 100 mm concrete block construction with a 100 mm partially filled cavity, as shown.
questionText:
(a) Calculate the U-value of the wall, given the construction has the following sequence and data: External render thickness 16 mm; Concrete block outer leaf thickness 100 mm; Clear cavity width 50 mm; Polystyrene insulation thickness 50 mm; Concrete block inner leaf thickness 100 mm; Internal plaster thickness 12 mm.
Thermal data of the external wall: Resistance of external surface (R) 0.048 m2 °C/W; Resistivity of external render (r) 2.170 m °C/W; Conductivity of concrete external blockwork (k) 1.440 W/m °C; Resistance of clear cavity (R) 0.170 m2 °C/W; Conductivity of insulation (k) 0.037 W/m °C; Conductivity of concrete internal blockwork (k) 1.440 W/m °C; Resistivity of internal plaster (r) 6.250 m °C/W; Resistance of internal surface (R) 0.122 m2 °C/W.

(b) Using the U-value of the wall obtained at 5(a) above and the following data, calculate the cost of heat lost annually through this wall: area of external wall 135 m2; average internal temperature 19 °C; average external temperature 5 °C; heating period 9 hours daily for 36 weeks per annum; cost of oil 94 cent per litre; calorific value of oil 37350 kJ per litre; 1000 Watts 1 kJ per second.

(c) It is proposed to upgrade the thermal properties of the above wall, to meet the Passive House standard, by fixing expanded polystyrene to the external surface, as shown. Given the thermal conductivity (k) of expanded polystyrene as 0.031 W/m°C, calculate the thickness of expanded polystyrene required to achieve a U-value of 0.15 W/m2 °C.

rows.contextNote: Eight resistances, 3 each, by R = T/k (or R = T × r for render and plaster): external surface 0.048 (given); render 0.016 × 2.170 = 0.035; external blockwork 0.1/1.44 = 0.069; clear cavity 0.170 (given); insulation 0.05/0.037 = 1.351; internal blockwork 0.1/1.44 = 0.069; plaster 0.012 × 6.25 = 0.075; internal surface 0.122 (given). All in m²°C/W.
Total resistance Rt = 1.939 m²°C/W.
U = 1 ÷ Rt = 1 ÷ 1.939 = 0.516 W/m²°C, with units.
Heat loss = U-value × area × temperature difference = 0.516 × 135 × (19 − 5) = 975.24 watts (joules per second).
Heating period = 60 × 60 × 9 × 7 × 36 = 8,164,800 seconds (2,268 hours).

rows.verbatim: Litres of oil for one year

rows.contextNote: Annual cost = 212.34 × €0.94 = €199.60. The scheme’s alternative one-line method gives the same €199.60.

rows.verbatim: Resistance for U- value for 0.15Wm2K (using R=1/U)
rows.contextNote: Required resistance = 1 ÷ 0.15 = 6.666 m²K/W.

rows.verbatim: Resistance from calculated U-value from part (a)
rows.contextNote: Existing resistance = 1 ÷ 0.516 = 1.939 m²K/W (the scheme prints the divisor as 0.156).
Difference = 6.666 − 1.939 = 4.727 m²K/W.
T = 4.727 × 0.031 = 0.146537 m: 147 mm of expanded polystyrene (146 or 147 mm accepted).

stem: “Global warming is now a generally recognised phenomenon and sustainability is recognised as being a necessity, not an option. One of the main culprits blamed for global warming is carbon dioxide (CO2), so it is worth taking a look at what can be done about it. CO2 is produced by each of us every day, and our personal carbon footprint is a measure of how many tonnes of CO2 are emitted directly or indirectly, as a result of the consumption of goods and services. When building your own home you should take every opportunity to build in the most sustainable way so as to minimise your own carbon footprint.” Adapted from: Building Your Own Sustainable and Energy Efficient House. by Henry Skates Published by: The Crowood Press Ltd. ISBN: 978-1-84797-258-3

questionText: Explain, with the aid of notes and freehand sketches, any five of the following: carbon monoxide alarm; grab rail; furniture castor; laminated safety glass; eaves gutter; balusters; sapwood; bridle joint; fluorescent lighting.

rows.contextNote: Explain any five of the nine terms. Each term is marked separately: primary communication of relevant information 6 and other communication 4, in notes or sketches (the scheme reserves no fixed split between them). Carbon monoxide alarm: detects carbon monoxide and sounds an alarm before dangerous levels build up in a room, preventing poisoning by a colourless, tasteless, odourless "silent killer". Grab rail: a safety rail, usually stainless steel, chromed or plastic-coated metal, giving support and balance, lessening fatigue and something to grip in a slip or fall. Furniture castor: a wheel with a fixing plate or screw, fitted to tables, chairs and desks for easy movement; made of cast iron, plastic, nylon, steel or aluminium. Laminated safety glass: glass that holds together when shattered, held by a polyvinyl butyral (PVB) or ethylene-vinyl acetate (EVA) interlayer between the sheets. Eaves gutter: fixed to the fascia, it collects rainwater from pitched or flat roofs and discharges it to an outlet or downpipe; cast iron, uPVC, aluminium, galvanised steel, copper or zinc. Balusters: vertical hardwood or softwood members between the string and the handrail, supporting the handrail; generally 38 × 38 or 44 × 44 mm, square or turned, no more than 100 mm apart. Sapwood: the outer, newer wood of a tree’s cross section, carrying the sap; lighter in colour, softer and less durable than heartwood. Bridle joint: a strong woodworking joint, tee or corner, used in furniture and frame construction, such as joining table rails to uprights. Fluorescent lighting: a low-pressure mercury-vapour discharge lamp whose ultraviolet light makes a phosphor coating glow; dearer to buy but cheaper to run; used in workplaces and homes.

stem: A house built in the 1970s has an uninsulated solid concrete ground floor, as shown, with a sand/cement fine screed finish.
questionText:
(a) Calculate the U-value of the uninsulated concrete ground floor, given the following data: Sand/cement fine screed thickness 50 mm; Concrete floor slab thickness 100 mm; Radon barrier thickness 0.25 mm; Sand blinding thickness 40 mm; Hardcore thickness 200 mm; Subsoil thickness 300 mm.
Thermal data of the concrete ground floor: Resistance of internal top surface of floor (R) 0.104 m2 °C/W; Resistivity of fine screed (r) 0.710 m °C/W; Conductivity of concrete floor slab (k) 1.280 W/m °C; Conductivity of radon barrier (k) 0.250 W/m °C; Conductivity of sand blinding (k) 0.160 W/m °C; Conductivity of hardcore (k) 1.350 W/m °C; Conductivity of subsoil (k) 1.600 W/m °C.

(b) Using the U-value of the concrete floor obtained at 5(a) above and the following data, calculate the cost of heat lost annually through the uninsulated concrete floor slab: dimensions of floor slab 6.0 metres × 12.0 metres; average internal temperature 21 °C; average temperature of subsoil 5 °C; heating period 10 hours daily for 38 weeks per annum; cost of oil 96 cent per litre; calorific value of oil 37350 kJ per litre; 1000 Watts 1 kJ per second.

(c) It is proposed to redesign the above floor and upgrade its thermal properties to meet the Passive House standard by including expanded polystyrene in the design of the floor. Given the thermal conductivity (k) of expanded polystyrene as 0.037 W/m °C, calculate the thickness of expanded polystyrene required to achieve a U-value of 0.15 W/m2 °C.

rows.contextNote: The calculation set out in a table of material, conductivity, resistivity, thickness and resistance.

rows.verbatim: Internal top surface resistance Fine screed Concrete floor slab Radon barrier Sand blinding Hardcore Subsoil
rows.contextNote: Seven resistances, 3 each, by R = T/k (or R = T × r for the screed): internal top surface 0.1040 (given); screed 0.05 × 0.71 = 0.0355; slab 0.1/1.28 = 0.0781; radon barrier 0.00025/0.25 = 0.0010; sand blinding 0.04/0.16 = 0.2500; hardcore 0.2/1.35 = 0.1481; subsoil 0.3/1.6 = 0.1875. All in m²°C/W.
Total resistance Rt = 0.8042 m²°C/W.

rows.verbatim: Calculation of U-value of ground floor
rows.contextNote: U = 1 ÷ Rt = 1 ÷ 0.8042 = 1.2434 W/m²°C, with units.
Heat loss = U-value × area × temperature difference = 1.2434 × 72 × 16 = 1432.3968 watts (joules per second).
Heating period = 60 × 60 × 10 × 7 × 38 = 9,576,000 seconds (2,660 hours).

rows.verbatim: Litres of oil for one year

rows.contextNote: Annual cost = 367.24 × €0.96 = €352.5. The scheme’s alternative one-line method gives the same €352.5.

rows.verbatim: Resistance for U- value for 0.15Wm2K using R=1/U
rows.contextNote: Required resistance = 1 ÷ 0.15 = 6.6666 m²K/W.

rows.verbatim: Resistance from calculated U-value from part (a)
rows.contextNote: Existing resistance = 1 ÷ 1.2434 = 0.8042 m²K/W.
T = 5.8624 × 0.037 = 0.2169088 m: 216.9 mm of expanded polystyrene (216 or 217 mm accepted).

rows.verbatim: Design of a passive house - any 2
rows.contextNote: Any two of the three printed items, each notes 4 and sketches 4 = 8. Space heating energy demand: the energy to keep 20 °C all year, at most 15 kWh/m²/a in a Passive House, set by insulation and airtightness; solar gain from well-placed glazing with shading against overheating. stem: Green design is about being green, rather than simply appearing to be green. So greening your house is about more than just buying all sorts of expensive ‘eco-bling’ and adding it to your house. Ironically, that could be just another display of consumerism. Rather, greening your house is about making responsible environmental choices based on what you want to do, what you can do and what you can afford. This means that - before we get into the minutiae of sustainable building materials - we should address some fundamentals, chief among which is the need to build modestly and source locally. From: contemporary design secrets: the art of building a house in the countryside Jane Burnside (2013) Published by: BOOKLINK. ISBN 978-1-906886-42-4

questionText: Explain, with the aid of notes and freehand sketches, any five of the following: smart meter; biscuit joint; earth rod; airtightness tape; evacuated tube; magnetic catch; roof-light window; aerated shower; LED lighting.

rows.contextNote: Explain any five of the nine terms. Each term is marked separately: primary communication of relevant information 6 and other communication 4, in notes or sketches (the scheme reserves no fixed split between them). Smart meter: records the electricity used in the home and shows its cost, giving awareness and control of energy use; it can send readings to the supplier and may also record water or gas. Biscuit joint: joins boards of different widths in modern furniture; a biscuit joiner cuts a groove in each edge, and glued pressed-beech biscuits are inserted before the boards are clamped. Earth rod: a copper or steel rod, usually 1200 mm long, driven outside the building and connected to the electrical system; it carries fault current and lightning to earth, preventing shock and fire. Airtightness tape: tape sealing joints in the structure — around windows, doors, floors, ceilings, joists, pipes and ducts — to prevent draughts and reduce heat loss. Evacuated tube: part of a solar panel: a vacuum glass tube around a copper heat pipe whose glycol fluid vaporises, rises to a header and heats the coil in the hot water cylinder. Magnetic catch: a catch for cabinet and wardrobe doors: a base unit with magnetised strips on the frame and a striking plate on the door, carefully aligned so they meet when the door closes. Roof light window: an opening window for sloping, flat or low-pitched roofs, double, triple or quadruple glazed, letting light into rooms in an attic development. Aerated shower: mixes air with the flow of water, cutting use to about 7 litres a minute against 12 for a traditional shower while keeping a comfortable flow; it saves water and energy. LED lighting: light-emitting diodes for domestic and commercial fittings, using about 90% less energy than halogen bulbs and lasting far longer, though dearer to buy.

stem: While there are undoubtedly many buildings whose heritage values dictate that they should be preserved unchanged, the reality is that few are of such importance that they and their settings are not capable of being remodelled to accommodate new uses - especially where they have outlived the functions for which they were constructed, and where adaptation and reuse is the most viable option for extending their lifespans and preserving the vitality of their urban locations. The alternative is to let them fall into disuse and disrepair, along with the ensuing deterioration of their urban environments. Adapted from: Use it or Lose it - Challenges in the Protection of Architectural Heritage – by Paul Keogh. VOL 6 IRISH ARCHITECTURE - THE RIAI ANNUAL REVIEW 2015/2016. ISBN: 978-0-9567493-5-2 Published by: The Royal Institute of Architects of Ireland, 8 Merrion Square, Dublin 2.
questionText: Discuss the above statement in detail.

rows.verbatim: Discussion – point 2 (4 for point, 6 for discussion)

rows.verbatim: Discussion – point 3 (4 for point, 6 for discussion)
rows.contextNote: Point 4 and discussion 6. Such as: reuse needs upgrading for heat, fire and universal access, while keeping the original legible and the changes reversible. Three distinct, well-argued points are needed.

stem: A dwelling house has a 400 mm external concrete block wall with a 200 mm full-fill insulated cavity. The ground floor is an insulated concrete floor with a 20 mm floating tongue-and-groove hardwood finish, as shown.
questionText:
(a) To a scale of 1:5, draw a vertical section through the strip foundation, the external wall and the ground floor. Show the typical construction details from the bottom of the foundation to a level 400 mm above finished floor. Show the position of the radon barrier and include four typical dimensions on your drawing. Show 1.0 metre width of floor.

(b) On your drawing, show the typical design detailing to prevent the formation of a thermal bridge at the junction of the external wall and the floor.

rows.verbatim: Any 9 of the above details ( 4 marks each)
rows.contextNote: Credit the best NINE acceptable details at 4 marks each, capped at 36. Marked details: 100 mm concrete path/ground level; DPC; 100 mm block outer leaf and 19 mm render; full-fill cavity insulation; wall tie; 100 mm block inner leaf and 13 mm plaster; skirting board; 20 mm floating timber floor; 150 mm concrete floor taped and sealed to the wall; 300 mm floor insulation; DPM/radon barrier; hardcore and sand blinding; concrete fill/foundation blocks; reinforced concrete foundation.
Four appropriate typical dimensions on the section, 1 each.

rows.verbatim: Perimeter insulation/thermal blocks/cavity insulation overlaps with floor insulation/flexible seal between floor and wall

stem: The owners of a house have decided to insulate their house over a number of years, starting with the attic space. The rafters and ceiling joists are 200 mm × 40 mm. The water storage tank is in the attic, as shown.
questionText:
(a) Draw a large freehand sketch of the attic space. On your sketch, show the typical design detailing necessary to insulate, to a high standard, each of the following: attic space; water storage tank and pipework.

(b) Discuss two reasons why the attic space is chosen as the first area to be insulated.

rows.contextNote: Ceiling joist 4, rafter 4 and insulation in two layers 4, as in the scheme’s model sketch.
The tank 4, its supports kept free of insulation 4, and insulation on top and sides 4.
Insulation on the expansion pipe 4 and other exposed pipes 4.
Quality of the sketches: excellent 8, good 6, fair 4.
Such as: the greatest heat loss, up to 30%, is through the roof; the most effective way to save energy.
A second, different reason. Such as: relatively easy for the home owner; lower bills, a better BER and a warmer house; the tank and pipes there must be insulated anyway.

stem: The sketch shows a wood burning stove which is combined with a solar collector to provide hot water for a dwelling house. Also shown are a dual-coil hot water cylinder and the expansion tank in the attic.
questionText:
(a) Draw a large freehand sketch of the given diagram and also include the main cold water storage tank in the attic. Show the pipework required to connect the stove to the cylinder. Include the following on your sketch: rising main and the main cold water storage tank; hot water cylinder and expansion pipe; stove and pipework from stove to cylinder; all necessary valves.

(b) On the same sketch, show also the pipework necessary to connect the solar collector on the roof to the cylinder.

(c) Discuss two advantages of including a solar collector to provide domestic hot water for a house.

rows.verbatim: Any 8 of the above details (4 marks each)
rows.contextNote: Credit the best EIGHT acceptable items at 4 marks each, capped at 32. Secondary circulation: 15 mm rising main; insulated storage tank; 22 mm cold feed to the cylinder; indirect cylinder; 22 mm expansion pipe. Primary circulation: wood burning stove; 28 mm primary flow and return; 22 mm cold supply and expansion pipe from the expansion tank; insulated expansion tank; overflows; valves.
Quality of the sketch: excellent 8, good 6, fair 4.
Such as: a solar controller; 22 mm flow from the panel to the cylinder and 22 mm return; a pump and isolator on the return; an expansion vessel and pressure release valve.
Such as: lower energy bills for hot water; low running costs once installed.
A second, different advantage. Such as: less CO₂ from fossil fuels; an independent source of energy; helps slow climate change.

(c) Discuss one reason why the planning authority allows the public to view all planning documents after a planning application is submitted.

rows.contextNote: Such as: a legal requirement when changing the front elevation of a house; it informs the public.
A second, different reason. Such as: it controls height, shape, design and location; prevents an unsafe sunspace; ensures it blends with its surroundings.

Three valid details, 5 each. Such as: what the site will look like when finished; the location of buildings and the new development; the septic tank and percolation area; the site notice position; north; a scale of 1:500.

Three valid details, 5 each. Such as: the planning authority; the applicant’s name; the location or address; the type of permission; the nature and extent of the development; whether it is a protected structure; where and when the application can be viewed.

questionText:
(a) Outline two specific safety precautions to be observed in the Construction Studies room in each of the following situations: using a scalpel to cut modelling card; carrying a chisel; using a contact adhesive.

(b) Using notes and freehand sketches, describe three specific safety precautions to be observed when turning a wooden bowl on a lathe, as shown. Give one reason for each safety precaution outlined.

rows.verbatim: Using a scalpel to cut modelling card
rows.contextNote: Two precautions, 4 each. Such as: a clean flat surface and cutting mat; a firmly held straight edge; always cut away from your hands; score lightly then repeat; cover scalpels and replace blunt blades.
Two precautions, 4 each. Such as: carry it down by your side with the edge towards the floor; never in a pocket; walk, never run.
Two precautions, 4 each. Such as: latex gloves and goggles; a well-ventilated area; avoid inhaling the fumes; keep away from heat; follow the instructions for use and storage.
Precaution and reason. Such as: the work properly secured to the faceplate, or it may come loose.
A second, different precaution and reason. Such as: rotate the piece by hand first so it clears the tool rest; set the correct speed, slow for big work.
A third, different precaution and reason. Such as: a visor against flying chips; long hair and loose cuffs tied up; know how to stop the lathe; sound wood free of defects.
