stem: A house in the vernacular tradition, as shown in the sketch, was built over 100 years ago without insulation and is now in need of significant refurbishment. The occupants have decided to refurbish the house on a step-by-step basis over a number of years.
questionText: A survey of the house reveals: external random rubble stone walls, 450 mm in thickness, with an internal and external lime render; traditional cut roof with natural slates; suspended timber ground floor. Select any two of the above areas and, using notes and freehand sketches, describe the steps involved in upgrading each area selected. Show how the refurbishment should be carried out in a manner that respects the character of the original house and ensures the reuse of materials.

rows.contextNote: Any two of the three printed areas, each note 6 and sketch 6 = 12. External random rubble wall: keep the wall breathable with no vapour barriers; hempcrete, wood fibre boards or lime plasters inside or out; a French drain against rising damp; layers progressively more permeable towards the outside. Traditional cut roof: minimal intervention: slates numbered, stored and reused; impermeable felt replaced with a vapour-diffuse membrane; only decayed parts of rafters spliced or replaced in the same timber; hygroscopic insulation such as sheep’s wool and wood fibre board; counter battens for ventilation. Suspended timber ground floor: floorboards numbered and lifted; sub-floor ventilation checked; decayed joists or boards replaced; insulation between the joists on netting or battens with a breather membrane; boards and skirting relaid as labelled.
The refurbishment respects the character of the original house, such as matching materials, profiles and the original roof plane.
Materials reused, such as numbered slates and floorboards relaid and decayed timber replaced only where needed.

questionText:
Using the following data, calculate the U-value of the insulated concrete ground floor: Concrete floor slab thickness 125 mm; Extruded polystyrene insulation thickness 200 mm; Damp proof membrane (DPM) thickness 0.30 mm; Sand blinding thickness 30 mm; Hardcore thickness 225 mm.
Thermal data of floor: Resistance of top surface of floor (R) 0.104 m2 °C/W; Conductivity of concrete (k) 0.160 W/m °C; Conductivity of polystyrene insulation (k) 0.031 W/m °C; Conductivity of damp proof membrane (DPM) (k) 0.450 W/m °C; Conductivity of sand blinding (k) 0.160 W/m °C; Conductivity of hardcore (k) 1.260 W/m °C.

rows.contextNote: The calculation set out in a table of material, conductivity, thickness and resistance.

rows.verbatim: Insulated concrete ground floor (9 points × 3 marks)
rows.contextNote: Six resistances, 3 each, by R = T/k: top surface 0.1040 (given); slab 0.125/0.160 = 0.7813; insulation 0.200/0.031 = 6.4516; DPM 0.00030/0.450 = 0.0006; sand blinding 0.030/0.160 = 0.1875; hardcore 0.225/1.260 = 0.1786. All in m²°C/W.
Total resistance, the sum of R = 7.70 m²°C/W.
U = 1/Rt = 1 ÷ 7.7 = 0.1298 W/m²K (1 mark for the formula).

questionText: Using the U-value of the concrete ground floor obtained at 5(a) above and the following data, calculate the cost of heat lost annually through the concrete ground floor: Dimensions of floor 13.0 metres × 7.0 metres; Average internal temperature 21°C; Average external temperature 7°C; Heating period 12 hours per day for 39 weeks per annum; Cost of oil 95 cent per litre; Calorific value of oil 37350 kJ per litre; 1000 Watts 1 kJ per second.

rows.contextNote: Heat loss = U-value × area × temperature difference = 0.1298 × 91 × 14 = 165.36 watts (joules per second).
Heating period = 12 × 7 × 39 = 3,276 hours = 11,793,600 seconds.

rows.verbatim: Litres of oil for one year
rows.contextNote: Oil = 1,950,190 ÷ 37,350 = 52.2 litres per year.

questionText: Using notes and freehand sketches explain any two of the following: sound absorption; sound reflection; reverberation time.

rows.contextNote: Any two of the three printed principles, each notes 6 and sketch 6 = 12. Sound absorption: the sound absorbed by surfaces and materials in a room: hard shiny surfaces absorb little and reflect, causing echo; soft carpets, curtains and furnishings absorb sound. Sound reflection: the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence, as with light; used to distribute sound evenly in a room, important in theatres. Reverberation time: the time for a sound to decline by 60 dB; it varies with the room’s size and furnishings; reflective surfaces give a longer time than soft ones.

questionText: Using notes and freehand sketches, discuss in detail the importance of any two of the following in the design of a Passive House: building form; indoor air quality; foundation design.

rows.verbatim: Design of a passive house - any 2
rows.contextNote: Any two of the three printed items, each note 5 and sketch 5 = 10. Building form: a simple, compact form with a surface-to-volume ratio of 0.7 or less: less material, easier to heat and make airtight; complex forms add wall area, cold bridges and wind chill. Indoor air quality: build tight and ventilate right: MHRV supplying filtered fresh air and extracting moist air from wet rooms; at most 0.6 air changes per hour; humidity 30–60%; CO₂ below 1000 ppm. Foundation Design: an insulated foundation to cut heat loss to the soil: high-density extruded polystyrene on blinded, compacted hardcore; a mesh-reinforced slab; a radon barrier.

stem: “Our common ground starts with the planet. As a species we have never been more vulnerable than we are today. The world is under stress and we are the cause of it. We are now at a tipping point and, as with all periods of great change, there is great opportunity. The world needs the way architects think, we should not keep ourselves aloof from the urgent situation we are in. The most resilient and sustainable form of human habitation is the town or the neighbourhood. We must build to create neighbourhoods. We must plan and design to avoid isolation and disconnection. We must design for what matters, which is ultimately happiness.” Adapted from: PRESIDENT’S INTRODUCTION - Michelle Fagan, President RIAI IRISH ARCHITECTURE, Vol. 3, 2012 / 2013. RIAI, 8 Merrion Square, Dublin 2. ISBN: 978-0-9567493-2-1
questionText: Discuss the above statement in detail.

rows.verbatim: Discussion – point 1 (4 for point, 6 for discussion)
rows.contextNote: Point 4 and discussion 6. Such as: the planet is under stress — climate change, flooding, diminishing fossil fuels and rising CO₂ at a tipping point.

rows.verbatim: Discussion – point 2 (4 for point, 6 for discussion)
rows.contextNote: Point 4 and discussion 6. Such as: architects leading a new paradigm of deep-green, nearly zero energy, beautiful homes rather than staying aloof.

rows.verbatim: Discussion – point 3 (4 for point, 6 for discussion)
rows.contextNote: Point 4 and discussion 6. Such as: towns and neighbourhoods as the most resilient habitation — living near work and leisure, avoiding isolated, energy-hungry one-off houses. Three distinct, well-argued points are needed.

questionText: Explain, with the aid of notes and freehand sketches, any five of the following: strip foundation; housing joint; laser beam; thermostatic valve; collar tie; radon sump; roof-light window; smart meter; external ramp.

rows.contextNote: Explain any five of the nine terms. Each term is marked separately: primary communication of relevant information 6 and other communication 4, in notes or sketches (the scheme reserves no fixed split between them). Strip Foundation: a simple, common and economical concrete foundation, reinforced with steel bars, supporting a solid or cavity wall centrally; typically three times the wall thickness wide and as thick as the wall; the load spreads at 45 degrees to the ground. Housing joint: a basic joint joining two pieces at right angles: a trench removed from one piece takes the other, glued for strength; used in cabinets, bookcases and shelving; simple, strong and easy to make. Laser beam: a light beam used in printers, cutting and welding and barcode scanning; on site a laser projector sends out the beam and a staff with an adjustable sensor detects it, giving levels at different points on the site or on internal walls. Thermostatic Valve: a valve fitted to a radiator in a central heating system, controlling its heat output to give the desired room temperature; inexpensive, it reduces heating costs and CO₂ emissions. Collar tie: a member in tension stretching from rafter to rafter, tying them into a triangle for structural stability; purlins may rest on it; typically 200 × 50 mm; it may form the ceiling in an attic conversion. Radon sump: a compartment placed centrally in the hardcore under the ground floor to collect radon gas through gaps in its walls; pipes from its connectors carry the gas outside the building, where it dissipates. Roof-light window: a window fitted in a sloping roof (or a special roof light for a flat roof), letting light and ventilation into an attic; double or triple glazed and highly insulated, fitting neatly into the roof surface; top or pivot hung. Smart meter: records the electricity used in the home and shows its cost at any time, giving the householder control; may be topped up with credit; can also record gas or water. External ramp: a sloping path for easy access for people with restricted mobility, wheelchairs and buggies: gradient 1:20, sections no longer than 9.0 m, at least 1200 mm clear width, non-slip, lit from the sides.

stem: A section through a triple-glazed, high performance wooden window is shown at A. The frame is a thermally broken, insulated frame as shown. A section through a traditional single-glazed solid wooden window is shown at B.
questionText: The traditional single-glazed solid wooden window shown at B has the following U-values: U-value of the solid wooden frame 0.317 W/ m2 °C; U-value of the single glazing 5.300 W/ m2 °C. Using the U-values of the high performance window frame and glazing unit obtained at 5(a) and the U-values of the traditional single-glazed wooden window given at 5(b) above, discuss the performance of both windows under the following headings: thermal properties; environmental considerations.

rows.contextNote: Such as: the thermally broken frame (0.178) is almost twice as efficient as the traditional frame (0.317), the insulation in line with the glazing; the triple-glazed unit (0.261) up to twenty times more efficient than single glazing (5.300), which loses about 25% of the heat; lower heat loss costs and more comfort.

rows.contextNote: Point 4 and discussion 6. Such as: the downstairs room used as a study, playroom or bedroom at no extra cost; a door opening into the bathroom; upstairs work done while the ground floor room is used.

rows.verbatim: Proximity to services (4 for point, 6 for discussion)
rows.contextNote: Point 4 and discussion 6. Such as: schools, shops and a doctor within walking or cycling distance; public transport to work, with no second car; a stronger sense of community; services nearby are more sustainable.

stem: The elevation and ground floor plan of a house are shown. The house has three bedrooms and a bathroom in the attic space. The external wall is of timber frame construction with a rendered concrete block outer leaf. The house is designed to have low environmental impact and be suitable for first-time buyers.
questionText:
(a) With reference to the design shown, discuss in detail, using notes and freehand sketches, three features of the design that contribute to the house having a low environmental impact.

(b) Discuss in detail the importance of each of the following when designing a house suitable for first-time buyers: modest in scale; easy to modify; proximity to services.

rows.contextNote: Note 5 and sketch 5. Such as: a steep pitched roof giving three bedrooms and a bathroom on a compact footprint; roof lights giving three times the daylight of dormers.
A second, different feature: note 5 and sketch 5. Such as: south-facing high-performance glazing and small north windows; a wood-burning stove on an internal chimney stack; rainwater harvesting.

A third, different feature: note 5 and sketch 5. Such as: solar panels on the south roof; the long elevation on an east–west axis; a flexible universal design; local timber frame and low-carbon GGBS concrete.

rows.verbatim: Modest in scale (4 for point, 6 for discussion)
rows.contextNote: Point 4 and discussion 6. Such as: a small footprint and site keep building, purchase and mortgage costs down; one room deep for solar gain; no corridors to heat; bedrooms in the attic; zoned heating.

rows.verbatim: Easy to modify (4 for point, 6 for discussion)
rows.contextNote: Point 4 and discussion 6. Such as: the downstairs room used as a study, playroom or bedroom at no extra cost; a door opening into the bathroom; upstairs work done while the ground floor room is used.

rows.verbatim: Proximity to services (4 for point, 6 for discussion)
rows.contextNote: Point 4 and discussion 6. Such as: schools, shops and a doctor within walking or cycling distance; public transport to work, with no second car; a stronger sense of community; services nearby are more sustainable.

questionText: A trial hole, as shown in the sketch, indicates a moderately firm clay subsoil for the foundations of a dwelling house. The external wall of the house is a 350 mm solid concrete block wall with an insulated cavity. Consideration is being given at the design stage to using either: a traditional strip foundation or a raft foundation. Show, using notes and annotated freehand sketches, the typical design detailing for each type of foundation. Recommend a preferred foundation for the house and give two reasons for your recommendation.

rows.contextNote: Notes 5 and sketches 5. Such as: a reinforced strip at least 600 mm down against frost heave; hardcore, sand blinding, radon barrier and insulation; cavity fill.
Notes 5 and sketches 5. Such as: a mesh-reinforced concrete raft on hardcore; radon barrier and insulation; DPC at least 150 mm above ground level.
The preferred foundation, strip or raft.
A reason matching the choice. Such as, strip: suited to moderately firm clay; easily constructed, filled and levelled.
A second, different reason. Such as, strip: economical in materials and labour; raft: suited to poor soils, spreads the load evenly and reduces settlement, and allows load-bearing walls anywhere.

questionText: Discuss in detail three best practice guidelines that should be observed to ensure the maximum strength of concrete in a foundation.

rows.contextNote: Such as: a level trench bottom free of loose soil; clean, correctly sized aggregates; batching by weight.
A second, different guideline. Such as: the correct water/cement ratio, about 0.6; reinforcement placed as designed with 75 mm cover; sulphate-resisting cement where needed.
A third, different guideline. Such as: compaction without excessive vibration; concrete not dropped from a height; cured for up to 28 days and protected from extreme heat or cold.

stem: A two-storey house, as shown in the drawing, is of timber frame construction with a rendered concrete block outer leaf. The chimney is also of rendered concrete block construction and both roofs are slated. Careful design detailing is required to prevent the penetration of dampness at the critical junctions circled in the drawing.
questionText: Select any three locations from those circled on the drawing and show, using notes and freehand sketches, the typical design detailing which will prevent the penetration of dampness at each location.

rows.contextNote: Any three of the four circled locations, each note 6 and sketch 6 = 12. Location 1: the chimney on the main roof: a lead back gutter welted under the slates; the roofing membrane carried under the battens and taped to the chimney; a cover flashing at the back of the chimney overhanging the lead gutter. Location 2: the window head: a stepped DPC so moisture cannot reach the inside leaf; an anti-capillary groove at the sash opening; a weather strip at the top of the window; mastic sealant around the window. Location 3: the window cill: the cill wrapped in DPC; a second layer of DPC around the cavity barrier; an anti-capillary groove in the cill; mastic sealant; airtight tape between the frame and the internal wall. Location 4: the lean-to roof against the wall: a stepped DPC; a cover flashing at the roof–wall junction; the roof membrane carried onto the wall and taped to the masonry.

questionText: Using notes and freehand sketches as appropriate, discuss in detail the importance of any two of the following in the design of a Passive House: building orientation; thermal mass; primary energy demand.

rows.contextNote: Any two of the three printed items, each note 6 and sketch 6 = 12. Building orientation: the glazed façade due south or within 30° of south to maximise solar gain, especially in winter; otherwise more insulation and careful fenestration are needed. Thermal mass: the ability of a material, usually the concrete floor, to absorb and store heat: it stores solar gain, stabilising the temperature against summer overheating and heating the home in winter; high heat capacity and density with moderate conductivity. Primary energy demand: the total energy for space and water heating, ventilation and all electricity, at most 120 kWh/m²a for certification (typically 60–70); electricity has a conversion factor of about 2.4.

rows.contextNote: A single-line plan of the given rooms.

rows.contextNote: Extract ducts from the kitchen, bathroom and utility and supply ducts to the living spaces and bedrooms, with the airflow shown in every duct, as in the scheme’s model plans.

rows.verbatim: Explanation of how the system works
rows.contextNote: Moist warm extract air and filtered outdoor air pass through a heat exchanger of thin plates without mixing; the outdoor air is warmed and supplied to the living spaces; a post heater in cold weather and a summer bypass; a sound attenuator.

stem: “It is worth questioning whether a large house built to passive standards but remote from schools, shops or workplace, may in the long term be less sustainable than a modestly-sized home built within walking or cycling distance from daily destinations. The cost of energy required to power but also to transport goods and people from place to place will increasingly form part of the debate on sustainability. Passive living is not just a factor of the energy rating of the fabric of the house, but of an holistic approach to how we as a society think about dwelling, about the reuse of existing space in the first instance and about the appropriateness of scale”. From House to Home: a long conversation - Orla Murphy, School of Architecture, UCD HOUSE - AN EXHIBITION OF 21ST CENTURY HOMES IN THE WEST OF IRELAND (2012) AVAYA: 25-29 Mervue Business Park, Mervue, Galway
questionText: Discuss the above statement in detail.

rows.verbatim: Discussion – point 1 (4 for point, 6 for discussion)
rows.contextNote: Point 4 and discussion 6. Such as: a remote house needs large amounts of energy and materials for services and roads, while a modest home near schools, shops and work is reached by walking, cycling or public transport.

rows.verbatim: Discussion – point 2 (4 for point, 6 for discussion)
rows.contextNote: Point 4 and discussion 6. Such as: oil and gas are finite and over a third of energy goes on transport; sustainability must look beyond the BER of the fabric to a holistic approach to living.

rows.verbatim: Discussion – point 3 (4 for point, 6 for discussion)
rows.contextNote: Point 4 and discussion 6. Such as: Ireland builds the largest houses in the EU while town centres decay; reuse existing buildings, build modest, compact, flexible deep-green homes. Three distinct, well-argued points are needed.
